semin-durr:2-2.t:
His saying: {ذِكْرُ}: there are three views on it. The first: it is a mubtadaʾ (subject) whose khabar (predicate) is omitted, its implied form being: "among what is recited to you is the mention …". The second: it is a khabar whose mubtadaʾ is omitted, its implied form being: "what is recited is the mention", or "this is the mention". The third: it is the khabar of the disjointed letters (al-ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭaʿa); this is the view of Yaḥyā ibn Ziyād [al-Farrāʾ]. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "This is far-fetched, because the khabar is the mubtadaʾ in meaning, and in the disjointed letters there is no mention of mercy, nor in the mention of mercy is their meaning."
The generality of readers read the ends of these disjointed letters with sukūn. Likewise some readers used to pause slightly on each letter, to stress distinguishing them from one another.
Al-Ḥasan read «كافُ» with ḍamma, as though he made it declinable, and made it a diptote because of being a proper name and feminine. The readers disagree about the imāla (inclination toward kasra) of «يا» and «ها» and about pronouncing them with tafkhīm (full, open vowel).
Some of them express tafkhīm as "ḍamma", just as they express imāla as "kasra"; I only mention this because their expression in this is misleading.
Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr and ʿĀṣim pronounced the dāl of «صاد» distinctly before the dhāl of «ذِكْرُ», because it is the original; the rest assimilated it into it. [Translator's note: printed «ذَكْرُ»; the lemma is «ذِكْرُ».]
The well-known [practice] is the concealment (ikhfāʾ) of the nūn of «عَيْن» before the ṣād, because it is close to it and they share the mouth [as place of articulation]; some pronounce it distinctly, because they are disjointed letters, the intention being to distinguish them [from one another].
«ذِكْرُ» is a maṣdar (verbal noun) in iḍāfa. It was said: annexed to its object, which is "the mercy"; and "the mercy" itself is also a maṣdar annexed to its agent, and «عبدَه» is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object), what makes it accusative being the [word] "mercy" itself; the agent of the mentioning then is not mentioned in words, the implied form being: "that Allah mentioned His showing mercy to His servant". It was also said: rather «ذِكْرُ» is annexed to its agent by extension of usage, and «عبدَه» is accusative by the [word] "mention" itself, the implied form being: "that the mercy mentioned His servant"; so He made the mercy figuratively one who mentions him.
«زكريَّا» is a badal (substitute) or ʿaṭf bayān (explicative apposition), or accusative by an implied «أَعْني» ("I mean").
Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar read — and al-Zamakhsharī transmitted it from al-Ḥasan — «ذَكَّرَ» as a past verb with doubling, and «رحمةَ» accusative, as a second object put before the first, which is «عبدَه»; the agent is either the pronoun of the Quran or the pronoun of the Creator, the Exalted. The implied form is: "that the recited Quran — or Allah — reminded His servant of His mercy", i.e. made the servant remember His mercy. On the figurative sense mentioned before, «رحمةَ ربك» may be the first object, the meaning being that Allah made the mercy remember the servant. It was also said: the origin is "reminded with mercy", and when the preposition was removed its genitive noun was made accusative; but there is no need for this.
Al-Kalbī read «ذَكَرَ» without doubling, as a past verb; «رحمةَ» accusative as the mafʿūl bihi; «عبدُه» nominative as the fāʿil (agent) of the verb before it; and «زكريَّا» nominative as explication or badal, or by an implied mubtadaʾ — this is the counterpart of implying the governor of the accusative in the first reading.
Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar read — according to what al-Dānī transmitted from him — «ذَكَّرْ» as an imperative verb, with «رحمةَ» and «عبدةَ» both accusative as two objects; [regarding] them, as preceded, each of them may be the first or the second object, with the interpretation mentioned before of making the mercy figuratively one who remembers. [Translator's note: as an imperative the verb would be «ذَكِّرْ», and «عبدةَ» is presumably «عبدَه».]

semin-durr:3-3.t: His saying: {إِذْ نادى}: on what governs its accusative there are three views. The first: it is «ذِكْرُ»; al-Ḥawfī mentioned nothing else. The second: it is «رحمة»; Abū al-Baqāʾ mentioned both views. The third: it is a badal (substitute) from «زكريَّا», a badal of inclusion (badal ishtimāl), because the time includes him. The like of this will come at His saying {واذكر فِي الكتاب مَرْيَمَ} [Maryam: 16] and similar places.

semin-durr:4-4.t:
His saying: {قَالَ رَبِّ}: this clause has no grammatical position, because it is an explanation (tafsīr) and clarification of His saying «نادى ربَّه»; for that reason the conjunction between them was left out, because of the strength of the connection.
His saying: «وَهَنَ»: the generality of readers read it with fatḥa on the hāʾ. Al-Aʿmash read it with kasra, and it was read with ḍamma; these are dialectal forms of this word. "The bone" was put in the singular to intend the genus, meaning that this genus, which is the pillar of the body and the strongest and hardest thing in it, has been struck by weakness; had it been put in the plural, it would have had another intent, namely that not some of his bones but all of them had weakened. Al-Zamakhsharī said this. It was also said: the singular is used and the plural intended, as in the poet's saying:
320 - 8- بها جِيَفُ الحَسْرى فأمَّا عِظامُها ... فبِيضٌ وأمَّا جِلْدُها فَصَلِيْبُ
(In it are the carcasses of the exhausted [camels]: as for their bones, they are white, and as for their skin, it is hard.)
i.e. their skins. And similar to it:
320 - 9- كُلوا في بعضِ بطنِكُم تَعِفُّوا ... فإنَّ زمانَكُمْ زَمَنٌ خَمِيصُ
(Eat to fill part of your belly and stay abstinent, for your time is a time of hunger.)
i.e. your bellies.
«مَنَّي» is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from «العَظْم». [Translator's note: i.e. «مِنِّي».] In it is a refutation of whoever says that the alif and lām may substitute for the pronoun annexed [to the noun], because they have been combined here, even though the origin is "my bone has weakened". Similar to it in indicating that is what they recited as evidence for what I have mentioned:
321 - 0- رَحِيبٌ قِطابُ الجَيْبِ منها رَفْيقَةٌ ... بجَسِّ النَّدامى بَضَّةُ المُتَجَرِّدِ
(Wide is the opening of her collar, gentle to the touch of the drinking companions, fair-skinned when unclothed.)
His saying: «شَيْباً»: on its accusative there are three views. The first — and it is the well-known one — is that it is a tamyīz (specification) transferred from the agent, since the origin is "the greyness of the head blazed". Al-Zamakhsharī said: "He likened grey hair, in its whiteness, its spreading in the hair and its pervading it and taking hold of it in every way, to the blazing of fire; then He expressed it as a metaphor (istiʿāra); then He attributed the blazing to the place of the hair and where it grows, which is the head; and He brought out the grey hair as a tamyīz; and He did not annex the head [to a pronoun], being content with the addressee's knowledge that it is the head of Zakariyyā. For this reason this sentence is eloquent and is testified to for its rhetorical excellence." End [of quote]. This is the metaphor of a sensible thing for a sensible thing, and the common feature is spreading and diffusion.
The second: it is a maṣdar (verbal noun) not from the verb's own root, for the meaning of «اشتعلَ الرأسُ» is "it became grey". [Translator's note: printed «على غيرِ الصَّدْرِ»; read as «على غير الصَّدْر/المصدر».]
The third: it is a maṣdar occurring in the place of a ḥāl, i.e. "being grey", or "having grey hair".
His saying: «بدُعائِك»: there are two views on it. The more apparent: the maṣdar is annexed to its object, i.e. "by my calling upon You". The second: it is annexed to its agent, i.e. "I have not been, by Your calling me to faith, wretched."

semin-durr:5-5.t:
His saying: {خِفْتُ الموالي}: the generality of readers read «خِفْتُ» with kasra on the khāʾ and sukūn on the fāʾ; it is a past verb attributed to the tāʾ of the speaker. «المَوالي» is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object), meaning that his kinsmen were the wicked of the Children of Israel, so he feared them for the religion. Al-Zamakhsharī said this.
Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "There must be an omission of a muḍāf, i.e. the absence of the kinsmen, or the injustice of the kinsmen."
Al-Zuhrī read it likewise, except that he made the yāʾ of «المَواليْ» quiescent. It has preceded that the fatḥa may be implied (muqaddar) on the yāʾ and wāw, and on this is the reading of Zayd ibn ʿAlī {تُطْعِمُونَ أَهْلِيكُمْ} [al-Māʾida: 89]. The clarification of this has preceded.
ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, Zayd ibn Thābit, Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ, Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar and ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn among others read «خَفَّتِ» with fatḥa on the khāʾ and the fāʾ doubled, and the tāʾ of the feminine, given kasra because of the meeting of two quiescent letters; and «المَوالِيْ» is its agent, meaning they passed away and died out.
His saying: {مِن وَرَآئِي}: in the reading of the majority this is attached to the verbal meaning contained in «المَوالي», i.e. those who will take charge of the affair after me. It is not attached to «خِفْتُ», because the meaning would be corrupted; this is on the basis that by «ورائي» is meant "behind me and after me". As for the reading «خَفَّتْ» with doubling, the adverbial phrase is attached to the verb itself, and «ورائي» means "before me". The meaning is: they dwindled away before him and passed on, and none of them remained through whom there could be strength and support. Al-Zamakhsharī mentioned these two meanings.
Al-mawālī: the cousins (sons of the paternal uncle). This is indicated by the poet's explaining them thus in his saying:
321 - 1- مَهْلاً بني عَمَّنا مَهْلاً مَواليَنا ... لا تَنْبُشوا بَيْنَنا ما كان مَدْفُوْنا
(Gently, sons of our uncle, gently, our kinsmen! Do not dig up between us what was buried.)
Another said:
321 - 2- ومَوْلَىً قد دَفَعْتُ الضَّيْمَ عنهُ ... وقد أمْسَى بمنزلةِ المَضِيْمِ
(And many a kinsman I have defended from wrong, when he had come to be in the position of the wronged.)
The majority read «ورائي» with madd (lengthening). Ibn Kathīr read — in one transmission from him — «وَرايَ» with shortening. This is not unlikely from him, for he shortened «شُرَكاي» in al-Naḥl, as preceded, and it will come that he read {أَنْ رَاْه اسْتَغْنى} in al-ʿAlaq; it is as though he preferred shortening to lengthening because of its lightness. But according to the Basrans it is not permissible in free speech [only in poetry].
{مِن لَّدُنْكَ} may be attached to «هَبْ». It may also be attached to an omitted [word] as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from «وَليَّاً», because it is originally an adjective of the indefinite noun and was put before it.

semin-durr:6-6.t:
His saying: {يَرِثُنِي وَيَرِثُ}: Abū ʿAmr and al-Kisāʾī read both verbs jussive (majzūm), as the answer to the command, since its implied form is: "if You grant, he will inherit". The rest read both nominative, as an adjective of «وليَّاً».
ʿAlī, the Commander of the Believers — may Allah be pleased with him — Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar, al-Jaḥdarī and Qatāda among others read «يَرِثُني» with the yāʾ of the absent [third person] and nominative, and «وأَرِثُ» attributed to the pronoun of the speaker. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: "In the speech there is fronting and postponement; the implied form is: he will inherit my prophethood if I die before him, and I will inherit his wealth from him if he dies before me." This was transmitted from al-Ḥasan.
ʿAlī also, Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Jaḥdarī read «يَرِثُني وارثٌ», making it an active participle, i.e. "an heir will inherit from me through him"; this is called al-tajrīd (abstraction) in the science of bayān.
Mujāhid read «أُوَيْرِثٌ», which is the diminutive of «وارِث»; the origin is وُوَيْرِث with two wāws. The first of them had to be changed into hamza because both are vowelled and come together at the beginning of a word, like «أُوَيْصِل», the diminutive of «واصل». The second wāw is a substitute for the alif of fāʿil. أُوَيْرِث is triptote. It should not be said that it ought to be a diptote because it has two causes, being an adjective and having the pattern of a verb — since it has the pattern of أُبَيْطِر, the imperfect of بَيْطَر — this being one of those cases where the noun is triptote in the non-diminutive form and diptote in the diminutive. That should not be said, because it is a clear error: for the pattern of «أُوَيْرِث» is fuwayʿil, not ufayʿil, unlike «أُحَيْمِر», the diminutive of «أَحْمَر». [Translator's note: printed «تصعير»; read as «تصغير».]
Al-Zuhrī read «وارِث» with kasra on the wāw; by this they mean imāla.
His saying: «رَضِيَّا»: a second object; it is faʿīl in the sense of fāʿil, and its origin is رَضِيْوٌ, because it is from al-riḍwān.

semin-durr:7-7.t:
His saying: {يحيى}: there are two views on it. The first: it is a foreign name with no derivation; this is the apparent view, and it is a diptote because of being a proper name and foreign. [Translator's note: printed «سامٌ»; read as «اسمٌ».] It was also said: rather it is transferred from the imperfect verb, as they named [people] Yaʿmur, Yaʿīsh and Yamūt — he is Yamūt ibn al-Muzarraʿ.
The clause in His saying {اسمه يحيى} is in the position of the genitive as an adjective of «غُلام», and likewise {لَمْ نَجْعَل}. «سَمِيَّا» is like His saying «رَضِيَّا» in iʿrāb and morphology, because it is from al-sumuww (height). In it is evidence for the view of the Basrans that al-ism (name) is from al-sumuww; had it been from al-wasm (marking), it would have been said "wasīman".

semin-durr:8-8.t:
His saying: {عِتِيّاً}: there are four views on it. The most apparent: it is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object), i.e. "I have reached extreme decrepitude of old age". On this view {مِنَ الكبر} may be attached to «بَلَغْتُ», or attached to an omitted [word] as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from «عِتِيَّا», because it is originally its adjective, as I have shown you its implied form. The second: it is a maṣdar (verbal noun) confirming the verb, because reaching old age is in its meaning. The third: it is a maṣdar occurring in the place of a ḥāl from the agent of «بَلَغْتُ», i.e. "being decrepit" or "having decrepitude". The fourth: it is a tamyīz (specification). On these three views «مِنْ» is redundant (zāʾida); Abū al-Baqāʾ mentioned this. The first is the [correct] way.
Al-ʿutuww has the pattern fuʿūl; it is the maṣdar of عَتا يَعْتُو, i.e. it dried and hardened. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It is dryness and stiffness in the joints and bones, like a withered stick; one says عَتا العُوْدُ وجَسا (the stick dried and stiffened). Or [the meaning is] I have reached of the stages and degrees of old age what is called ʿitiyy." By his saying "or I have reached" he means that it may be from عتا يَعْتُو, i.e. it became corrupt.
The origin is عُتُوْوٌ with two wāws. Two wāws after two ḍammas were felt to be heavy, so the tāʾ was given kasra for lightness; then the first wāw turned into yāʾ because of its sukūn and the kasra before it; so a yāʾ and a wāw came together, the first of them with sukūn, so the wāw was changed into yāʾ and the first yāʾ was assimilated into it. This weakening (iʿlāl) occurs in the singular, like this, and in the plural, like «عِصِيّ»; except that in the singular the common case is keeping it sound, as in His saying «وعَتَوْا عُتُوَّاً كبيراً», though it may be weakened as in this verse; and in the plural the common case is the weakening, though it may be kept sound, as in "إنكم لتنظرون في نُحُوّ كثيرة". And they said فُتِيّ and فُتُوّ.
The two brothers read «عِتِيَّا», «صِلِيَّا», «بِكِيَّا» and «جِثِيَّا» with kasra on the first radical, for vowel harmony; the rest with ḍamma, according to the original.
ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd read the first [letter] of «عَتِيَّا» and «صَلِيَّا» with fatḥa, making them two maṣdars on the pattern faʿīl, like al-ʿajīj and al-raḥīl.
ʿAbd Allāh and Mujāhid read «عُسِيَّا» with ḍamma on the ʿayn and kasra on the undotted sīn. The derivation and morphology of this word have preceded in al-Aʿrāf.

semin-durr:9-9.t:
His saying: {كذلك}: on the position of this kāf there are two views. The first: it is nominative as the khabar (predicate) of an implied mubtadaʾ (subject), i.e. "the matter is thus"; the pause is then on «كذلك», and another clause is begun. The second: it is in the position of the accusative. Abū al-Baqāʾ gave its implied form as: "I will do the like of what you asked", this being an allusion to what he asked for; so he made what governs its accusative implied, and apparently it is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object).
Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Or it is accusative by «قال», and «ذلك» points to something vague explained by {هُوَ عَلَيَّ هَيِّنٌ}; similar to it is {وَقَضَيْنَآ إِلَيْهِ ذَلِكَ الأمر أَنَّ دَابِرَ هَؤُلآءِ مَقْطُوعٌ مُّصْبِحِينَ} [al-Ḥijr: 66]. Al-Ḥasan read {وهُوَ عَلَيَّ هَيِّنٌ}, and this can only be explained according to the first view, i.e. the matter is as you said, and it is, despite that, easy for Me. Another view: «ذلك» points to what preceded of Allah's promise, not to the saying of Zakariyyā. And «قال» is omitted in both readings" — "in both readings" meaning the reading of the generality and the reading of al-Ḥasan — "i.e. He said: 'It is easy for Me'; He said: 'And it is easy for Me'. And if you wish, you need not intend it, because Allah is the One addressing, and the meaning is that He said that, and His promise and His word are the truth."
There is unsteadiness in this speech. Its upshot comes back to [saying] that the second «قال» is what makes the kāf accusative. His saying "and «قال» is omitted" is a derivation on the view that the speech is complete at «قال ربك», and one begins with His saying {هُوَ عَلَيَّ هَيِّنٌ}. His saying "and if you wish, you need not intend it" means: you need not intend the implied saying, because Allah is the One speaking that.
The apparent sense of some people's words is that the first «قال» is attributed to the pronoun of the angel. Ibn Jarīr stated this explicitly, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya followed him. Al-Ṭabarī said: "The meaning of His saying «قال كذلك» is: the two matters you mentioned, the barren wife and old age, are so; but your Lord has said … And the meaning in my view is: the angel said: 'Thus', i.e. in this state, 'your Lord has said: It is easy for Me'." End [of quote]. [Translator's note: «ولكم قال ربُّكِ» as printed; read as «ولكن قال ربُّك».]
Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī read «عَلَيِّ» with kasra on the yāʾ of the speaker, as in the poet's saying:
321 - 3- عَلَيَّ لعمروٍ نِعْمَةٌ بعد نِعْمةٍ ... لوالدِه ليسَتْ بذاتِ عَقَارِبِ
(I owe ʿAmr favour after favour, for his father's sake, favours without stings.)
They recited it with kasra. I have discussed this question exhaustively at the reading of Ḥamza {بِمُصْرِخِيِّ}. [Translator's note: printed «أَمْنَعْتُ»; read as «أَشْبَعْتُ» ("I discussed exhaustively").]
His saying: {وَقَدْ خَلَقْتُكَ}: this is a resumptive clause. The two brothers read «خَلَقْناك», attributing it to the One who magnifies Himself; the rest «خَلَقْتُكَ» with the tāʾ of the speaker.
His saying: {وَلَمْ يَكُ شَيْئاً} is a ḥāl (circumstantial) clause. The meaning of denying his being a "thing" is: a thing of any account, as in the poet's saying:
321 - 4-. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... إذا رَأَى غيرَ شَيْءٍ ظَنَّه رَجُلاً
(… when he sees a nothing, he thinks it a man.)
And they said: "I wondered at a nothing." It is also possible that He said that because the non-existent is not a thing.

semin-durr:10-10.t:
His saying: {سَوِيّاً}: a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the agent of «تُكَلِّمَ». From Ibn ʿAbbās: «سَوِيَّاً» is a description of the nights, meaning "complete"; its accusative is then as a naʿt (adjective) of the adverb of time. The majority read the mīm of «تُكَلِّم» accusative, making it [«أَنْ»] the one that governs the accusative.
Ibn Abī ʿAbla [read] with the nominative, making it the one lightened from the heavy [«أنّ»], its noun being an omitted pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), and «لا» separating. Its verification has preceded.

semin-durr:11-11.t:
His saying: {أَن سَبِّحُواْ}: «أَنْ» may be explicative (mufassira) of «أَوْحى», or maṣdariyya (forming a verbal noun), being the object of the revealing. {بُكْرَةً وَعَشِيّاً} are two adverbs of time for the glorifying. «بُكْرَة» is triptote because it is not intended as a proper name; if it were intended as a proper name it would be diptote — whether a specific time is intended by it, as in «لأسيرنَّ الليلةَ إلى بكرةَ» (I shall travel tonight until early morning), or not intended, as in «بكرةُ وقتُ نشاط» (early morning is a time of energy) [because its being a proper name is generic, like Usāma]. The same applies to «غدوة» in all of this.
Ṭalḥa read «سَبَّحوه» with the hāʾ of the pronoun. Also from him: «سَبِّحُنَّ», attributing the verb to the pronoun of the group, emphasised with the heavy [nūn]; it is like His saying {لَّيَقُولُنَّ مَا يَحْبِسُهُ} [Hūd: 8]. Its morphology has preceded. [Translator's note: as an imperative the word would be «سَبِّحوه».]

semin-durr:12-12.t: His saying: {بِقُوَّةٍ}: a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the agent or the object, i.e. "you being clothed with strength" or "it being clothed with strength". «صَبِيَّا» is a ḥāl from the hāʾ of «آتيناه».

semin-durr:13-13.t:
{وَحَنَاناً}: it may be a mafʿūl bihi (direct object) conjoined to «الحُكْمَ», i.e. "and We gave him tenderness". Al-ḥanān is mercy and gentleness. Abū ʿUbayda recited:
321 - 5- تحنَّنْ عليَّ هداك المليكُ ... فإنَّ لكلِّ مقامٍ مَقالا
(Have tenderness for me — may the King guide you — for every situation has its fitting word.)
He said: "Its most frequent use is in the dual, as in their saying: ḥanānayka; and the poet's saying:
321 - 6-. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... حَنَانَيْكَ بعضُ الشرِّ أهونُ مِنْ بعضِ
(… mercy upon mercy! Some evil is lighter than other.)"
Abū al-Baqāʾ allowed it to be a maṣdar (verbal noun), as though he means the maṣdar occurring in supplication, like saqyan and raʿyan; so its accusative is by an implied verb, like its sisters. It may also be nominative as the khabar (predicate) of an implied mubtadaʾ (subject), like {فَصَبْرٌ جَمِيلٌ} [Yūsuf: 18] and {سَلاَمٌ عَلَيْكُمْ} [al-Aʿrāf: 46, al-Raʿd: 24, al-Zumar: 73], in one of the two views. Sībawayh recited:
321 - 7- وقالَتْ حَنانٌ ما أَتَى بك هَهنا ... أذو نَسَبٍ أَمْ أنتَ بالحَيِّ عارِفُ
(She said: Mercy! What has brought you here? Are you of kin, or do you know the tribe?)
And Allah the Exalted is called Ḥanān, as He is called "Raḥīm". Al-Zamakhsharī said: "That is by way of metaphor."
{مِّن لَّدُنَّا} is its adjective.
[Translator's note: the source says "it may be a mafʿūl bihi" and then gives the other views without explicit numbering; the nominative possibility is presented here as a further view about the word, as in the source.]

semin-durr:14-14.t:
His saying: {وَبَرّاً}: it may be conjoined to the khabar (predicate) of «كان», i.e. "he was God-fearing, dutiful". It may also be accusative by an implied verb, i.e. "and We made him dutiful". Al-Ḥasan read «بِرَّاً» with kasra on the bāʾ in both places. Its interpretation is clear, like His saying {ولكن البر مَنْ آمَنَ} [al-Baqara: 177], whose interpretation has preceded. «بِوالِدَيْهِ» is attached to «بَرَّاً».
«عَصِيَّا»: its pattern may be faʿūl, the origin being عَصُوْيٌ, and there was done to it what is done to its counterparts; faʿūl is for intensiveness, like ṣabūr. Its pattern may also be faʿīl, which is also for intensiveness.

semin-durr:16-16.t:
His saying: {إِذِ انتبذت}: on «إذ» there are several views. The first: it is accusative by «اذكُرْ», on the basis that it has left the adverbial use, since it is impossible for it to remain with its past [meaning] while what governs it is explicitly future. The second: it is accusative by an omitted [noun] annexed to "Maryam", its implied form being: "and mention the report of Maryam", or "her story", "when she withdrew"; so «إذ» is accusative by that "report" or "story". The third: it is accusative by an omitted verb, its implied form being: "and He made clear", i.e. Allah the Exalted; so it is another sentence. This is as Sībawayh said regarding His saying {انتهوا خَيْراً لَّكُمْ} [al-Nisāʾ: 171]; and it is stronger with an adverb, even though it is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object) [there]. The fourth: it is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from that implied muḍāf, i.e. "the report of Maryam" or "the story of Maryam"; this is far-fetched. Abū al-Baqāʾ said this. The fifth: it is a badal (substitute) from «مريمَ», a badal of inclusion (badal ishtimāl). Al-Zamakhsharī said: "because times include what is in them; and in it [is the point] that the intent of mentioning Maryam is to mention this time of hers, because this wondrous story occurred in it."
Abū al-Baqāʾ said — after reporting this view from al-Zamakhsharī: "It is far-fetched, because a time, when it cannot be a ḥāl of a concrete entity, nor a khabar (predicate) about it, nor an adjective of it, cannot be a badal from it." This is open to objection, because the invalidity of what he mentioned does not entail the invalidity of substitution. Do you not see [an example] like «سُلِبَ زيدٌ ثوبُه» (Zayd was robbed of his garment)? «ثوبُه» cannot validly be made a khabar about «زيد», nor a ḥāl from him, nor an adjective of him; and yet it is a badal of inclusion.
The sixth: «إذ» means the maṣdariyya «أَنْ», as in your saying «لا أُكْرِمُك إذ لم تكرِمْني», i.e. "because you do not honour me"; on this view the badal of inclusion is good, i.e. "and mention Maryam: her withdrawing". Abū al-Baqāʾ mentioned this.
Al-intibādh is iftiʿāl from al-nabdh, which is casting away; its explanation has preceded.

semin-durr:17-17.t:
The majority read the rāʾ of «رُوْحِنا» with ḍamma; it is that by which they live. Abū Ḥaywa and Sahl read it with fatḥa, i.e. that in which there is rest (rāḥa) for the servants, as in His saying {فَرَوْحٌ وَرَيْحَانٌ} [al-Wāqiʿa: 89]. Al-Naqqāsh reported that «رُوْحَنَّا» was read with the nūn doubled, and he said: it is the name of one of the angels.
His saying: {بَشَراً سَوِيّاً}: a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the agent of «تَمَثَّلَ». What permitted the ḥāl to occur as an underived (jāmid) noun is its being qualified: since the indefinite noun was qualified, it occurred as a ḥāl.

semin-durr:19-19.t:
His saying: {لأَهَبَ}: Nāfiʿ and Abū ʿAmr read «لِيَهَبَ» with yāʾ, and the rest «لأَهَبَ» with hamza. In the first, the apparent sense is that the pronoun is for the Lord, i.e. "that the Lord may grant". It was also said: the origin is «لأَهَبَ» with hamza, and the hamza was only changed into yāʾ for lightening, because it has fatḥa after a kasra; so the two readings agree. This is far-fetched. As for the second, the pronoun is for the speaker, and the angel is meant by it; he attributed it to himself because he is a means in it. It is also possible that the pronoun is for Allah the Exalted, by way of reported speech with an omitted [verb of] saying. What strengthens the view before it is that in some copies of the Quran [there is]: «أَمَرَني أَنْ أَهَبَ لك» ("He commanded me to grant you").
And His saying: {إِن كُنتَ تَقِيّاً} [Maryam: 18]: its jawāb (apodosis) is omitted, or it is what came before.

semin-durr:20-20.t: His saying: {بَغِيّاً}: on its pattern there are two views. The first — the view of al-Mubarrad — is that its pattern is faʿūl, the origin being بَغُوْيٌ; the yāʾ and wāw came together, and what is well-known was done to it. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "For that reason the tāʾ of the feminine was not attached, just as it is not attached in ṣabūr and shakūr." Al-Zamakhsharī transmitted from Abū al-Fatḥ [Ibn Jinnī] that it is faʿīl; he said: "Had it been faʿūl, it would have been said بَغُوٌ, as one says: فلان نَهُوٌ عن المنكر (So-and-so is a great forbidder of evil)"; and he did not follow it with any disapproval. As for whoever says it is faʿīl: is it in the sense of fāʿil (agent) or in the sense of mafʿūl (patient)? If it is in the sense of fāʿil, it ought to have the tāʾ of the feminine, like امرأةٌ قديرةٌ وبَصيرة. This was answered thus: it is in the sense of relation (nasab), like ḥāʾiḍ and ṭāliq, i.e. "one possessing baghy (unchastity)". Abū al-Baqāʾ, when he made it in the sense of fāʿil, said: "The tāʾ is also not attached because it is for intensiveness"; so he made the reason for not attaching it its being for intensiveness. This is worth nothing. And if it is said that it is in the sense of mafʿūl, then the absence of the yāʾ is clear. [Translator's note: «الياء» as written; the tāʾ (of the feminine) is evidently meant.]

semin-durr:21-21.t:
His saying: {كذلك}: its counterpart has preceded.
His saying: «وَلِنَجْعَلَه»: it may be a reason whose effect is omitted, its implied form being: "in order to make him a sign for people, We did that". It may also be conjoined to an omitted reason, its implied form being: "that We may make clear by it Our power, and that We may make him a sign". The pronoun refers back to the boy. The noun of «كان» is latent in it, i.e. "and the boy was" — i.e. his creation and bringing into existence was — "a matter that must be".

semin-durr:22-22.t:
His saying: {فانتبذت بِهِ}: the preposition and its genitive noun are in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial), i.e. she withdrew while he was accompanying her, as in the poet's saying:
321 - 8-. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... تَدْوْسُ بنا الجَماجِمَ والتَّرِيْبا
(… she treads, with us [riding her], upon skulls and breastbones.)

semin-durr:23-23.t:
His saying: {فَأَجَآءَهَا}: the basic use of «جاء» is to be transitive to one object by itself; when the hamza enters it, analogy requires it to be transitive to two. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Except that its usage changed after the transfer to the meaning of al-iljāʾ (compelling). Do you not see that you do not say: جِئْتُ المكانَ وأَجَاءَنيهِ زيدٌ (I came to the place and Zayd brought me to it), as you say: بَلَغْتُه وأَبْلَغَنِيْه (I reached it and he made me reach it)? Its counterpart is «آتى», since it is used only for giving, and you do not say: أتيت المكانَ وآتانِيه فلان." Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "The origin is «جاءها», then it was made transitive by the hamza to a second object, and was used in the sense of «أَلْجَأَها» (compelled her)."
The Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] said: "His saying and the saying of [others], that «أجاءها» means «أَلْجَأَها», needs a transmission from the authorities of language who have inductively studied this in the speech of the Arabs. Al-ijāʾa indicates the absolute [sense of bringing], so it fits what is in the sense of compelling and what is in the sense of free choice, as when you say «أَقَمْتُ زيداً» (I made Zayd stand up): your making him stand may be by force or by choice. As for his saying 'Do you not see that you do not say …' to the end: whoever holds that making transitive by the hamza is analogical permits that even if it was not heard; and whoever forbids it — this has been heard in «جاء», so he permits it. As for his comparing that with «آتى», it is not a correct comparison, because he built it on [the assumption] that its hamza is for transitivity and that its origin is «أتى»; rather «آتى» is one of those built on afʿala. Had it been transferred from «أتى» transitive to one object, that one object would have been the second object, and the agent the first, when you make it transitive by the hamza: you say «أتى المالُ زيداً» (the wealth came to Zayd) and «آتى عمروٌ زيداً المالَ» (ʿAmr gave Zayd the wealth); so the construction differs by transitivity, because «زيداً» according to the grammarians is the first object and «المالُ» the second object, whereas according to what al-Zamakhsharī mentioned it would have been the reverse. This indicates that it is not as he said. Also, «آتى» is synonymous with «أَعْطَى», so it differs in terms of its indication of meaning. As for his saying 'and you do not say: أتيت المكانَ وآتانِيْه', this is not granted; rather you do say «أتيتُ المكانَ» as you say «جئت المكان». The poet said:
321 - 9- أَتَوْا ناري فقلتُ مَنُوَّنَ أنتُمْ ... فقالوا: الجنُّ قلتُ عِمُوا ظَلاما
(They came to my fire, and I said: Who are you? They said: The jinn. I said: Good evening to you!)
And whoever holds making transitive by the hamza to be analogical says «آتانيه»." These objections which the Shaykh raised against him have obvious answers, so we will not lengthen [the discussion] by mentioning them. [Translator's note: printed «ظاهرُه الأجوبة»; read as «ظاهرةُ الأجوبة». Where the Shaykh's quotation ends is not marked in the source.]
The majority read «فَأَجَاءَها», i.e. compelled her and drove her; from this is the poet's saying:
322 - 0- وجارٍ سارَ مُعْتَمِداً إليكم ... أَجَاْءَتْهُ المَخافةُ والرَّجاءُ
(And many a protégé journeyed, making for you, driven to you by fear and hope.)
Ḥammād ibn Salama read «فاجَأَها», with an alif after the fāʾ and a hamza after the jīm, from al-mufājaʾa (surprising), on the pattern of قابَلَها. It is also read with two pure alifs, as though they lightened the hamza after the jīm; and likewise it was transmitted with bayna bayna (the hamza between hamza and alif).
The majority read the mīm of «المَخاض» with fatḥa; it is the pain of childbirth. It was transmitted from Ibn Kathīr with kasra on the mīm. It was said: they have one meaning. It was also said: the one with fatḥa is a noun of the verbal noun (ism maṣdar), like al-ʿaṭāʾ and al-salām, and the one with kasra is a maṣdar (verbal noun) like al-qitāl and al-liqāʾ; and fiʿāl has come from a single [agent], like al-ʿiqāb and al-ṭirāq. Abū al-Baqāʾ said this. The mīm is a radical, because it is from تَمَخَّضَتِ الحامِلُ تتمخَّضُ (the pregnant woman went into labour).
{إلى جِذْعِ}, in the reading of the generality, is attached to «أَجاءها», i.e. drove her to it. In the reading of Ḥammād it is attached to an omitted [word], because it is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the object, i.e. "it surprised her as she leaned against the trunk of the palm tree".
His saying: «نَسْيَاً»: the majority read it with kasra on the nūn, sukūn on the sīn and a pure yāʾ after it. Ḥamza, Ḥafṣ and a group read with fatḥa on the nūn. The one with kasra is fiʿl in the sense of mafʿūl (patient), like al-dhibḥ (what is slaughtered) and al-ṭiḥn (what is ground); its meaning is the insignificant thing whose nature is to be forgotten, like a peg, a rope, a menstrual rag and the like.
Ibn al-Anbārī said: "Whoever reads with kasra, it is a noun for what is forgotten, as al-naqṣ is a noun for what is lacking; and the one with fatḥa is a maṣdar standing in place of the adjective." Al-Farrāʾ said: "They are two dialects, like al-watr and al-witr; the kasra is dearer to me."
Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī read «نِسْئاً» with kasra on the nūn and the hamza in place of the yāʾ. Also transmitted from him and from Bakr ibn Ḥabīb al-Sahmī is fatḥa with the hamza. They said: it is from نَسَأْتُ اللَّبَنَ, when you pour water into milk so that it is consumed in it; so the one with kasra is likewise the thing consumed, and the one with fatḥa is a maṣdar, just as that was from forgetting.
Ibn ʿAṭiyya transmitted from Bakr ibn Ḥabīb «نَسَا» with fatḥa on the nūn and the sīn and shortened, like ʿaṣā, as though he made faʿal in the sense of mafʿūl, like al-qabaḍ in the sense of al-maqbūḍ (what is seized).
«مَنْسِيَّاً» is a naʿt (adjective) by way of intensiveness; its origin is مَنْسُوْي, and it was assimilated. Abū Jaʿfar and al-Aʿmash read «مِنْسِيَّاً» with kasra on the mīm, for harmony with the kasra of the sīn; they did not take the quiescent letter into account, because it is a barrier that is not impenetrable, as in their saying «مِنْتِن» and «مِنْخِر».

semin-durr:24-24.t:
His saying: {مِن تَحْتِهَآ}: the two brothers, Nāfiʿ and Ḥafṣ read the mīm of «مِنْ» with kasra and «تحتِها» genitive, as a preposition and its genitive noun. The rest read it with fatḥa and «تحتَها» accusative. The first reading requires that the agent of «نادَى» be latent, and there are two interpretations of it. One: it is Gabriel, and the meaning of his being {مِن تَحْتِهَآ} is that he was in a place lower than her. This is indicated by the reading of Ibn ʿAbbās, «فناداها مَلَكٌ مِنْ تحتها» (so an angel called her from below her), where he stated it explicitly. On this view there are two views on {مِن تَحْتِهَآ}: one, that it is attached to the calling, i.e. the call came from this direction; the second, that it is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the agent, i.e. he called her while he was below her.
The second interpretation: the pronoun is for Jesus, i.e. the newborn called her from beneath her skirt. The preposition-phrase has the two views: being attached to the calling, or to an omitted [word] as a ḥāl. The second is clearer.
In the second reading «مَنْ» is a relative noun and the adverb is its ṣila (relative clause); and what is meant by the relative is either Gabriel or Jesus.
His saying: {أَلاَّ تَحْزَنِي}: «أَنْ» may be explicative (mufassira), because it is preceded by what has the meaning of saying; on this view «لا» is prohibitive, and the dropping of the nūn is due to the jussive. Or it may be the [«أَنْ»] that governs the accusative, «لا» then being negating, and the dropping of the nūn due to the accusative. The position of «أنْ» is then either accusative or genitive, because it is with the omission of the preposition, i.e. "he called her with such-and-such". The pronoun in «تحتها» is either for Maryam, peace be upon her, or for the palm tree; the first is more appropriate, so that the two pronouns agree.
His saying: «سَرِيَّا»: it may be a first object, and «تحتك» a second object, because it [«جعل»] means "made into". It may also mean "created", so «تحتك» is then a dependent (laghw) adverbial.
On al-sarī there are two views. The first: it is the man of high rank, from سَرُوَ يَسْرُو like شَرُف يَشْرُف, so he is sarī. Its origin is سَرِيْوٌ, and it was weakened as sayyid was weakened, so its third radical is wāw. What is meant by it in the verse is Jesus son of Maryam, peace be upon him. «سَرِيّ» is pluralised as «سَراة» with fatḥa on the sīn, and as «سُرَواء» like ẓurafāʾ; both are irregular plurals; rather, the analogy of its plural is «أَسْرِياء», like ghaniyy and aghniyāʾ. It was also said: al-sarī is from سَرَوْتُ الثوبَ, i.e. I took it off, and سَرَوْتُ الجُلَّ عن الفَرَس, i.e. I took the cover off the horse; as though the sarī has taken off his garment, unlike the one who wraps himself up (al-muddaththir, al-mutazammil). Al-Rāghib said this.
The second: it is a small stream; «فكُلي واشربي» fits this. Its derivation is from سَرَى يَسْرِي, because the water flows (yasrī) in it; on this view its third radical is yāʾ. They recited, by Labīd:
322 - 1- فتوسَّطا عُرْضَ السَّرِيِّ فَصَدَّعا ... مَسْجورةً مُتَجاوِزاً قُلاَّمُها
(The two of them went into the middle of the stream's breadth and split their way through a brimming [pool] whose reeds were crowded together.)

semin-durr:25-25.t:
His saying: {وهزى إِلَيْكِ بِجِذْعِ}: the bāʾ in «بِجِذْعِ» may be redundant (zāʾida), like it in the saying of the Exalted: {وَلاَ تُلْقُواْ بِأَيْدِيكُمْ} [al-Baqara: 195] [and the poet's saying]:
322 - 2-. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... . . . . . . . . . . . لا يَقْرَأْن بالسُّوَر
(… they do not recite the sūras.)
Al-Ṭabarī recited:
322 - 3- بوادٍ يَمانٍ يُنْبِتُ السِّدْرَ صَدْرَه ... وأَسْفَلُه بالمَرْخِ واشَّبَهانِ
(In a Yemeni valley whose upper part grows lote-trees, and whose lower part [grows] markh and shabahān.)
i.e. "shake the trunk of the palm tree". It is also possible that the object is omitted and the preposition-phrase is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from that omitted [object], its implied form being: "and shake toward you ripe dates being on the trunk of the palm tree". It is also possible that this is construed according to the meaning, since the implied form is: "shake the fruit by shaking the trunk", i.e. shake the trunk. Al-Zamakhsharī inclined to this, for he said: "Or [the meaning is] perform the shaking, as in the poet's saying:
322 - 4-. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... . . . يَجْرَحْ في عراقيبِها نَصْلي
(… my blade wounds their hamstrings.)"
The Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] said: "In this verse and in the saying of the Exalted {واضمم إِلَيْكَ جَنَاحَكَ} [al-Qaṣaṣ: 32] there is what goes against the rule established in grammar: that the verb of an attached pronoun does not pass over to its [own] attached pronoun except in the chapter of ẓanna (verbs of thinking) and in the two words faqada and ʿadima. One does not say ضَرَبْتَكَ or ضَرَبْتُني, meaning "you struck yourself" and "I struck myself"; one only uses al-nafs (self) for this. The ruling of what is governed by a preposition is the ruling of the accusative, so one does not say هَزَزْتَ إليك, nor زيدٌ هَزَّ إليه. For that reason the grammarians made «عن» and «على» nouns in the saying of Imruʾ al-Qays:
322 - 5- دَعْ عنك نَهْباً صِيْحَ في حُجُراتِه ... ولكنْ حَديثاً ما حديثُ الرواحلِ
(Leave aside the plunder that was cried out about in its quarters; but tell a tale — what is the tale of the riding camels?)
and the saying of the other:
322 - 6- هَوَّنْ عليكَ فإنَّ الأمورَ ... بِكَفِّ الإِلهِ مقادِيْرُها
(Take it easy, for the measures of all affairs are in the hand of God.)
Their being nouns is established by the entry of the preposition on them in the saying:
322 - 7- غَدَتْ مِنْ عليهِ بعدما تَمَّ ظِمْؤُها ... تَصِلُّ وعن قَيْضٍ ببَيْداءَ مَجْهَلِ
(She flew off from upon it after her thirst-interval was complete, rattling [with thirst], and from the eggshells in a trackless desert.)
and the saying of the other:
322 - 8- فقُلْتُ للرَّكْبِ لَمَّا أَنْ عَلا بِهِمْ ... مِنْ عَنْ يمينِ الحُبيَّا نظرةٌ قَبْلُ
(I said to the riders, when [the road] rose with them on the right of al-Ḥubayyā: one look, first!)
As for «إلى», it is a particle without disagreement, so it is not possible for it to be a noun like «عَنْ» and «على»." Then he answered that «إليك» in the two verses is not attached to the verb before it, but is attached to an omitted [word] by way of clarification, its implied form being: "I mean: toward you". He said: "As they interpreted that in His saying {لَكُمَا لَمِنَ الناصحين} [al-Aʿrāf: 21] in one of the views."
I say: there are two other answers to that. One: the verb that is prohibited [from passing over] to the attached pronoun is only where the verb falls upon that pronoun and the pronoun is its locus, as in «دَعْ عنك» and «هَوِّنْ عليك»; but the shaking and the drawing in do not fall upon the kāf, so there is nothing objectionable. The second: the speech involves the omission of a muḍāf, its implied form being: "shake toward your side and direction", and "draw in toward your side and direction".
His saying: «تُساقِطْ»: Ḥamza read «تَسَاقَطْ» with fatḥa on the tāʾ, the sīn undoubled and fatḥa on the qāf. The rest — except Ḥafṣ — likewise, except that they doubled the sīn. Ḥafṣ [read] with ḍamma on the tāʾ, the sīn undoubled and kasra on the qāf.
So the origin of the reading of those other than Ḥafṣ is «تَتَساقط» with two tāʾs, the imperfect of «تساقَطَ». Ḥamza dropped one of the two tāʾs for lightness, as in «تَنَزَّلُ» and «تَذَكَّرون», and the rest assimilated the tāʾ into the sīn.
The reading of Ḥafṣ is the imperfect of «ساقَطَ».
Al-Aʿmash and al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib read «يَسَّاقَطْ» like the group, except that it is with the lower-dotted yāʾ; he assimilated the tāʾ into the sīn, since the origin is يتساقط; so it is the imperfect of «اسَّاقط», whose origin is يَتَساقط; it was assimilated and the connecting hamza was brought in, like «ادَّارَأ» from تَدَارَأَ.
Three readings were transmitted from Abū Ḥaywa. Masrūq agreed with him in the first, which is «تُسْقِط» with ḍamma on the tāʾ, sukūn on the sīn and kasra on the qāf, from أَسْقَط. The second is likewise, except that it is with the lower-dotted yāʾ. The third is likewise, except that he made «رُطَبٌ جَنِيٌّ» nominative as the agent.
It was also read «تَتَساقط» with two upper-dotted tāʾs, which is the origin of the reading of the group; and «تَسْقُط» and «يَسْقُط» with fatḥa on the tāʾ and yāʾ, sukūn on the sīn and ḍamma on the qāf, with "the ripe dates" made nominative as the agent. And you give [these] verbs what agrees with them in the preceding readings. For whoever reads with the upper-dotted tāʾ, the verb is attributed either to the palm tree, or to the fruit understood from the context, or to the trunk; and the feminine of its verb is permissible because it is annexed to a feminine, so it is like the poet's saying:
322 - 9-. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... كما شَرِقَتْ صدرُ القناةِ من الدَّم
(… as the upper part of the lance chokes with blood.)
and like the reading «تَلْتَقِطْه بعض السيارة». For whoever reads with the lower-dotted yāʾ, the pronoun is for the trunk; it was also said: for the fruit indicated by the context.
As for the accusative of «رُطَباً», it does not go beyond being a tamyīz (specification), or a preparatory (muwaṭṭiʾa) ḥāl if the verb before it is intransitive, or a mafʿūl bihi (direct object) if the verb is transitive; and the intelligent [reader] refers each thing to what suits it among the readings. Al-Mubarrad allowed a strange view on its accusative: that it is a mafʿūl bihi of «هُزِّيْ». On this view the question belongs to the chapter of tanāzuʿ (contention of two governors) in some readings — namely where the verb in them is transitive — and the question is one of giving government to the second, with omission from the first.
Ṭalḥa ibn Sulaymān read «جِنِيَّاً» with kasra on the jīm, for harmony with the kasra of the nūn.
Al-ruṭab is a generic noun of ruṭaba, unlike «تُخَم», which is [the plural] of tukhama. The difference: they consistently treat it [al-ruṭab] as masculine, saying "it (huwa) is al-ruṭab", and that one [al-tukham] as feminine, saying "it (hiya) is al-tukham"; so they made «الرطب» masculine considering the genus, and «التُّخَم» feminine considering plurality. This is a subtle distinction. It is pluralised as «أَرْطاب» irregularly, like rubaʿ and arbāʿ. Al-ruṭb is what is cut before it dries and withers; al-ruṭab was specified for the fresh among dates. One says أَرْطَبَ النخلُ, like أَتْمَرَ and أَجْنَى.
Al-janiyy: what is ripe and fit for picking. It is faʿīl in the sense of mafʿūl; it was also said: in the sense of fāʿil, i.e. fresh. Al-janā and al-janiyy are also what is gathered of honey. أَجْنَى الشجرُ: its fruit ripened; أَجْنَتِ الأرضُ: its yield became abundant. From this was borrowed "جَنَى فلانٌ جنايةً" (So-and-so committed a crime), just as "اجْتَرَم جريمةً" was borrowed. [Translator's note: printed «كابَ»; read as «طابَ» ("was ripe/good").]

semin-durr:26-26.t:
His saying: {وَقَرِّي عَيْناً}: «عَيْناً» is accusative as a tamyīz (specification) transferred from the agent, since the origin is "let your eye be cool". The generality of readers read the qāf of «قَرِّيْ» with fatḥa, as an imperative from قَرَّتْ عَيْنُه تَقَرُّ, with kasra on the ʿayn [middle radical] in the past and fatḥa in the imperfect.
It was also read with kasra on the qāf; this is the dialect of Najd, who say قَرَّتْ عينُه تَقِرُّ, with fatḥa on the middle radical in the past and kasra in the imperfect. The well-known [usage] is that the one with kasra on the middle radical in the past is for the eye, and the one with fatḥa for the place: one says قَرَرْتُ بالمكانِ أَقِرُّ به (I settled in the place), and one may say قَرِرْتُ بالمكانِ with kasra. This will come at the saying of the Exalted: {وَقَرْنَ فِي بُيُوتِكُنَّ} [al-Aḥzāb: 33]. [Translator's note: the description of the two patterns here (kasra in the past for the eye, fatḥa for the place) is as written; it does not fully match the forms just given for the Najdī dialect.]
On describing the eye thus there are two interpretations. The first: it is taken from al-qurr, which is cold: that is because when the eye's owner rejoices, its tears are cool, i.e. cold, and when he grieves they are hot. For that reason they said in cursing someone: "May Allah make his eye hot", and in praying for him: "May Allah make his eye cool". How sweet is the saying of Abū Tammām:
323 - 0- فأمَّا عيونُ العاشِقينَ فَأُسْخِنَتْ ... وأمَّا عيونُ الشامتينَ فَقَرَّتِ
(As for the eyes of the lovers, they were made hot [with tears]; as for the eyes of the gloaters, they were cooled.)
The second: it is taken from istiqrār (settling), and the meaning is: Allah gave him what makes his eye settle, so that it does not look longingly to anything else.
His saying: {فَإِمَّا تَرَيِنَّ}: the conditional «إنْ» entered upon the redundant «ما» for emphasis, and was assimilated into it, and written joined. The morphology of «تَرَيِنَّ» has preceded. The generality of readers read [it] with a pure yāʾ with kasra. Abū ʿAmr read in one transmission «تَرَئِنَّ» with a hamza with kasra in place of the yāʾ; likewise «لَتَرَؤُنَّ» was transmitted from him, replacing the wāw with a hamza. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "This is from the dialect of those who say لَبَأْتُ بالحَجِّ and حَلأْتُ السَّوِيْقَ" — meaning with hamza — "and that is because of a kinship between the hamza and the soft letters." Ibn Khālawayh was bold against Abū ʿAmr and said: "It is an error (laḥn) according to most grammarians."
Abū Jaʿfar, the reader of Medina, Shayba and Ṭalḥa read «تَرَيْنَ» with a quiescent yāʾ and a light [undoubled] nūn. Ibn Jinnī said: "It is irregular." I say: because the jussive-governor should have had an effect and the nūn of the nominative should have been dropped, as in the saying of al-Afwah:
323 - 1- إمَّا تَرَيْ رَأْسِيَ أَزْرَى به ... ماسُ زمانٍ ذيٍ انتكاثٍ مَؤُؤْسِ
(If you see my head, [know that] it has been disgraced by the wearing of a time of reversals, a corrupting [time].)
And it had no effect here, irregularly. This is a counterpart of the saying of the other:
323 - 2- لولا فَوارسُ مِنْ نُعْمٍ وأُسْرَتِهِمْ ... يومَ الصُّلَيْفاءِ لم يُوفُوْنَ بالجارِ
(Were it not for horsemen of Nuʿm and their kin on the day of al-Ṣulayfāʾ, they would not have kept faith with the protégé.)
He did not give «لم» its effect, and kept the nūn of the nominative.
«من البشر» is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from «أحداً», because if it came after it, it would be an adjective. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "Or an object", meaning that it is attached to the verb itself before it.
His saying: «فَقُولِيْ»: between this jawāb (apodosis) and its condition is an omitted clause, its implied form being: "If you see any human being and he asks you to speak, then say". By this implied [clause] we are freed from a difficulty, namely that her saying {فَلَنْ أُكَلِّمَ اليوم إِنسِيّاً} is speech, so it would be a contradiction, since she would have spoken to a human being with this speech. Its answer is what preceded. It was also said: what is meant by His saying «فقُولي» to the end is that it is by gesture. This is worth nothing. Rather the meaning is: "I shall not speak today to any human being after this speech."
Zayd ibn ʿAlī read «صِياماً» instead of «صوماً»; both are maṣdars (verbal nouns).

semin-durr:27-27.t:
His saying: {فَأَتَتْ بِهِ قَوْمَهَا تَحْمِلُهُ}: «به» is in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the agent of «أَتَتْ», i.e. she came accompanied by him, as in "he came with his clothes", i.e. clothed in them. The bāʾ may also be attached to the coming. As for «تَحْمِلُه», it may be a second ḥāl from the agent of «أَتَتْ», or a ḥāl from the hāʾ in «به». The apparent sense of Abū al-Baqāʾ's words is that it is a ḥāl from the pronoun of Maryam and Jesus together; this is open to objection. [Translator's note: printed «تَحَمُّلُه»; the Quranic word is «تَحْمِلُه».]
His saying: «شيئاً»: a mafʿūl bihi (direct object), i.e. "you have done"; or a maṣdar (verbal noun), i.e. a kind of coming, «فَرِيَّاً». Al-fariyy: a tremendous matter; it is said of good and evil. It was also said: al-fariyy is the strange. It was also said: the fabricated. From the first is the ḥadīth describing ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him: "I have not seen a genius doing his work (yafrī fariyyahu)." Al-fary is cutting leather for stitching and mending, and al-ifrāʾ is spoiling it. In the proverb: "He came cutting the cut (yafrī al-fariyy)", i.e. doing a tremendous deed. The poet said:
323 - 3- فَلأَنْتَ تَفْرِيْ ما خَلَقْتَ وبَعْ ... ضُ القومِ يَخْلُقُ ثم لا يَفْري
(Indeed you cut what you have measured, while some people measure and then do not cut.)
Abū Ḥaywa read, according to what Ibn Khālawayh transmitted from him, «فَرِيْئاً» with hamza; and according to what Ibn ʿAṭiyya transmitted, «فَرْياً» with sukūn on the rāʾ.

semin-durr:28-28.t:
ʿUmar ibn Lajaʾ read {مَا كَانَ أَباكِ امرؤ سَوْءٍ}, making the indefinite the noun [of kāna] and the definite the khabar (predicate), as in the poet's saying:
323 - 4-. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... يكونُ مِزاجُها عَسَلٌ وماءُ
(… its mixture being honey and water.)
[And as in the poet's saying:]
3235 -. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... ولا يَكُ مَوْقِفٌ مِنْكِ الوَدَاْعا
(… and let not a halting with you be the farewell.)
Here it is better, because of the presence of iḍāfa (genitive construct) in the noun.

semin-durr:29-29.t:
The saying of the Exalted: {فَأَشَارَتْ}: al-ishāra (pointing) is well-known; it is with the hand, the eye and other things. Its alif is from a yāʾ. They recited, by Kuthayyir:
323 - 0- فقلتُ وفي الأحشاءِ داءٌ مُخامِرٌ ... ألا حَبَّذا يا عَزُّ ذاك التَّشايُرُ
(I said, while in my innards was a lingering illness: How lovely, O ʿAzza, is that exchange of signs!)
His saying: {مَن كَانَ فِي المهد صَبِيّاً}: on this «كان» there are several views. The first: it is redundant (zāʾida); this is the view of Abū ʿUbayd, i.e. "how shall we speak to one who is in the cradle?". On this view «صَبِيَّا» is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the latent pronoun in the preposition-phrase that occurs as the ṣila (relative clause). Abū Bakr [Ibn al-Anbārī] rejected this view — I mean its being redundant — on the grounds that had it been redundant it would not have made the khabar accusative, while this one has made «صَبيَّا» accusative. This rejection is rejected by what I have mentioned, namely its being accusative as a ḥāl, not as a khabar.
The second: it is complete (tāmma), meaning "occurred" and "came into existence"; the implied form is: "how shall we speak to one who has come into existence as a child?", and «صَبِيَّاً» is a ḥāl from the pronoun in «كان».
The third: it means «صار» (became), i.e. "how shall we speak to one who has become, in the cradle, a child?"; on this view «صَبِيَّا» is its khabar. So it is like the poet's saying:
323 - 7-. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... قَطا الحَزْن قد كانَتْ فِراخاً بُيُوضُها
(… sand-grouse of the rugged ground whose eggs had become chicks.)
The fourth: it is the incomplete (nāqiṣa) [kāna] in its proper sense, indicating the conjunction of the clause's content with past time without implying discontinuation, as in the saying of the Exalted: {وَكَانَ الله غَفُوراً رَّحِيماً} [al-Nisāʾ: 96]; for that reason it is described as synonymous with «لم تَزَلْ» ("has not ceased"). Al-Zamakhsharī said: "«كان» is for placing the content of the clause in an unspecified past time, suitable for the near and the distant. Here it is for the near one specifically; what indicates it is the meaning of the speech, and that it is set out to express astonishment. Another view: «نُكَلِّمُ» is the narration of a past state, i.e. how was it ever known before Jesus that a child in the cradle spoke to people, that we should speak to him?"
As for «مَنْ», the apparent [view] is that it is a relative noun meaning "who". Making it an indefinite noun qualified [by what follows] is weak, i.e. "how shall we speak to a person" or "a newborn". Al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj allowed it to be conditional, with «كان» meaning «يكنْ»; the jawāb (apodosis) of the condition is then either preceding, namely «كيف نُكَلِّم», or omitted because this indicates it, i.e. "whoever is a child in the cradle, how shall we speak to him?". On this view it is in the position of the nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject), and on what preceded it is in the position of the accusative by «نكلِّم». If it is said that «كان» is redundant, does it carry a pronoun or not? There is disagreement about this. Whoever allows it argues from the poet's saying:
323 - 8- فكيف إذا مَرَرْتَ بدارِ قومٍ ... وجيرانٍ لنا كانوا كرامِ
(So how [is it] when you pass by the abode of a people, and neighbours of ours who were noble?)
where the wāw is made nominative by it. Whoever forbids it interprets the verse as meaning that it is not redundant, and that its khabar is «لنا», put before it, and the adjective and the qualified noun were separated by the clause.
Abū ʿAmr assimilates the dāl [of «المهد»] into the ṣād [of «صبيا»]; most hold that it is concealment (ikhfāʾ).

semin-durr:31-31.t:
The saying of the Exalted: {أَيْنَ مَا كُنتُ}: this is conditional. Its jawāb (apodosis) is either omitted, indicated by what preceded, i.e. "wherever I am, He has made me blessed", or it is what precedes, according to whoever holds that view. It cannot be interrogative, because it would then require that what precedes it govern it, while interrogative nouns have the right to the head of the sentence; so it must be conditional, because it is confined to these two meanings.
His saying: «ما دُمْتُ»: «ما» is maṣdariyya ẓarfiyya (forming a verbal noun of duration), and the precedence of [«ما»] before «دام» is a condition for its operating. The implied form is: "for the duration of my remaining alive". Ibn ʿAṭiyya transmitted from ʿĀṣim and a group that they read «دُمْتُ» with ḍamma on the dāl, and from Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and the people of Medina «دِمت» with kasra. We have not seen this from anyone else, and it is not found in the books of the mutawātir and irregular readings that we have in hand; so it may be that he came upon it in some strange copy of the Quran. There is no doubt that «دام» has two dialectal forms: one says دُمْتَ تَدُوْم, which is the higher dialect, and دِمْتَ تَدام, like خِفْتَ تَخاف; this is as preceded for you in مات يموت and ماتَ يَمات.

semin-durr:32-32.t:
The saying of the Exalted: {وَبَرّاً}: the generality of readers read it with fatḥa on the bāʾ. There are two interpretations of it. The first: it is accusative, conjoined to «مباركاً», i.e. "and He made me dutiful". The second: it is accusative by an implied verb. This was preferred over the first because [in the first] there is a long separation by the clause of the enjoining and what is attached to it.
It was also read «بِرَّاً» with kasra on the bāʾ: either with the omission of a muḍāf, or by way of intensiveness in making him the maṣdar (verbal noun) itself. It has preceded in al-Baqara that it may be an adjective on the pattern fiʿl. Al-Zahrāwī and Abū al-Baqāʾ reported that it was read with kasra on the bāʾ and the rāʾ. Its explanation: it is conjoined to «الصلاة», i.e. "and He enjoined upon me prayer, zakāt and dutifulness". «بوالَديَّ» is attached to al-barr or al-birr. [Translator's note: the source prints «بوالَديَّ» ("to my two parents"), whereas the Quranic text of this verse is «بِوَالِدَتِي» ("to my mother").]

semin-durr:33-33.t:
His saying: {والسلام}: the alif and lām in it are for the previously known (al-ʿahd), because its word preceded in His saying {وَسَلاَمٌ عَلَيْهِ} [Maryam: 15]; so it is like His saying {كَمَآ أَرْسَلْنَآ إلى فِرْعَوْنَ رَسُولاً فعصى فِرْعَوْنُ الرسول} [al-Muzzammil: 15–16], i.e. that peace which was directed to Yaḥyā is directed to me. Al-Zamakhsharī said — after mentioning what I have set out: "The correct [view] is that this definiteness is an allusion (taʿrīḍ) to the curse upon those who accused Maryam, peace be upon her, and her enemies among the Jews. Its verification: the lām is for the genus; so when he said 'and the genus of peace is upon me specifically', he alluded that its opposite is upon you. Its counterpart is {والسلام على مَنِ اتبع الهدى} [Ṭā Hā: 47]."
His saying: {يَوْمَ وُلِدْتُّ}: accusative by the [sense of] being established contained in «عليَّ». It is not permissible to make it accusative by «السَّلام», because of the separation between the maṣdar (verbal noun) and what it governs. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read «وَلَدَتْ», making it a past verb attributed to the pronoun of Maryam, the tāʾ being for the feminine. «حَيَّاً» is an emphatic (muʾakkida) ḥāl (circumstantial).

semin-durr:34-34.t:
The saying of the Exalted: {ذلك عِيسَى ابن مَرْيَمَ قَوْلَ الحق}: «عيسى» may be the khabar (predicate) of «ذلك»; or it may be a badal (substitute) or ʿaṭf bayān (explicative apposition), with «قولُ الحق» its khabar. «قولُ الحق» may also be the khabar of an implied mubtadaʾ (subject), i.e. "it is the word of …". «ابن مريم» may be a naʿt (adjective), a badal, a bayān or a second khabar.
ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza and Ibn ʿĀmir read «قولَ الحق» accusative, and the rest nominative. The nominative is on what has preceded. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Its being nominative is as a khabar after a khabar, or a badal." The Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] said: "What he mentioned can only be by majāz (figurative usage) in [the word] qawl, namely that by it is meant the Word of Allah, because an utterance cannot be the person."
As for the accusative: it may be a maṣdar (verbal noun) confirming the content of the clause, as in your saying: «هو عبدُ الله الحقَّ لا الباطِلَ» (he is ʿAbd Allāh — truly, not falsely), i.e. I say the word of truth; al-ḥaqq is then truthfulness, and it is of the annexation of the qualified noun to its adjective, i.e. the true word, as in His saying {وَعْدَ الصدق} [al-Aḥqāf: 16], i.e. the true promise. It may also be accusative as praise, i.e. by al-Ḥaqq is meant the Creator, the Exalted, and «الذي» is an adjective of "the Word" if Jesus is meant by it; he is called "a word" (qawl) as he is called "a word" (kalima), because he arose from it. It was also said: it is accusative by an implied «أعني» ("I mean"). It was also said: it is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from «عيسى». This is supported by what was transmitted from al-Kisāʾī in explaining the nominative: that it is an adjective of Jesus.
Al-Aʿmash read «قالُ» with ḍamma on the lām; this is also the reading of Ibn Masʿūd. Al-Ḥasan read «قُوْلُ» with ḍamma on the qāf and on the lām. These are maṣdars of «قال»: one says قال يَقُولُ قَوْلاً وقالاً وقُوْلاً, like al-rahb, al-rahab and al-ruhb. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "Al-qāl is a noun [of the verbal noun], like al-qīl; and «قُولُ الحق» with ḍamma on the qāf was reported, like «الرُّوْح»; it is a dialectal form of it." I say: the apparent [view] is that these are all maṣdars, none of them being a noun of the verbal noun, as its determination preceded regarding al-rahb, al-rahab and al-ruhb.
Ṭalḥa and al-Aʿmash read «قالَ الحقُّ», making «قال» a past verb and «الحقُّ» its agent, by which the Creator, the Exalted, is meant; i.e. Allah, the Truth, said: Jesus is the Word of Allah. His saying {الذي فِيهِ يَمْتُرُونَ} is then the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ.
ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, al-Sulamī, Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind, and Nāfiʿ and al-Kisāʾī in one transmission from each, read «تَمْتَرون» with the tāʾ of address; the rest with the yāʾ of the absent [third person]. «تَمْتَرُون» is taftaʿilūn, either from al-mirya, which is doubt, or from al-mirāʾ, which is disputation.

semin-durr:35-35.t: The discussion of the accusative of «فيكونَ» and what has been said about it has preceded.

semin-durr:36-36.t:
The saying of the Exalted: {وَإِنَّ الله}: Ibn ʿĀmir and the Kufans read «وإنَّ» with kasra on «إنَّ», as resumptive. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy {إِنَّ الله} with kasra, without the wāw.
The rest read it with fatḥa, and there are several views on it. The first: it is with the omission of the preposition, attached to what comes after it, the implied form being: "and because Allah is my Lord and your Lord, worship Him", like the saying of the Exalted: {وَأَنَّ المساجد لِلَّهِ فَلاَ تَدْعُواْ مَعَ الله أَحَداً} [al-Jinn: 18]; the meaning is: because of His oneness, obey Him. Al-Zamakhsharī took this view, following al-Khalīl and Sībawayh.
The second: it is conjoined to «الصلاةِ», the implied form being: "and He enjoined upon me prayer, and that Allah …". Al-Farrāʾ took this view, and Makkī mentioned nothing else. It is supported by what is in the copy of Ubayy, «وبأنَّ اللهَ ربي», with the preposition bāʾ overt. This view was considered far-fetched because of the many separations between the two conjoined items. As for the bāʾ appearing in the copy of Ubayy, it does not give preference to this, because it is the bāʾ of causation; the meaning is: "because Allah is my Lord and your Lord, worship Him"; so it is like the lām.
The third: «أنَّ» and what follows it are conjoined to «أمراً», which is accusative by «قَضَى», the implied form being: "and when He decrees a matter, and decrees that Allah is my Lord and your Lord". Abū ʿUbayda mentioned that from Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ. People considered the correctness of this transmission from Abū ʿAmr unlikely, because he is of such eminence in knowledge and understanding as would prevent him from this view. That is because if it is conjoined to «أمراً», it necessarily falls within the domain of the condition with «إذا»; but His being — Blessed and Exalted is He — our Lord is not restricted by any condition at all; rather He is our Lord absolutely. They attributed this slip to Abū ʿUbayda, [who] was weak in grammar, and they counted errors against him; perhaps this is one of them.
The fourth: it is in the position of the nominative as the khabar (predicate) of an implied mubtadaʾ (subject), its implied form being: "and the matter is that Allah is my Lord and your Lord". This was mentioned from al-Kisāʾī; there is no need for this implication.
The fifth: it is in the position of the accusative, conjoined to «الكتاب» in His saying «قال: إني عبد الله آتاني الكتابَ», on the basis that those addressed by it are the contemporaries of Jesus, peace be upon him, and the one saying it to them is Jesus. From Wahb: Jesus charged them that "Allah is my Lord and your Lord". This proponent said: whoever reads the hamza with kasra will have conjoined {إِنَّ الله} to his saying «إني عبدُ الله», so it falls within the domain of the saying; and the clauses from His saying {ذلك عِيسَى ابن مَرْيَمَ} to their end are parenthetical clauses. This is extremely far-fetched.

semin-durr:37-37.t: The saying of the Exalted: {مِن مَّشْهِدِ}: «مَشْهد» is mafʿal, either from al-shahāda (testimony) or from al-shuhūd, which is presence. «مَشْهد» here may be meant as time, place or maṣdar (verbal noun). If it is from al-shahāda and time is meant by it, its implied form is: "from the time of the testimony"; if place is meant, its implied form is: "from the place of the testimony of a day"; if the maṣdar is meant, its implied form is: "from the testimony of that day", and that their tongues, hands and feet, the angels and the prophets testify against them. If it is from al-shuhūd, which is presence, its implied form is: "from the attendance of the reckoning and recompense on the Day of Resurrection", or "from the place of attendance in it", which is the Standing, or "from the time of attendance". When it is a maṣdar in its two preceding states, its annexation to the adverb [of time] is by extension of usage (ittisāʿ), like His saying {مالك يَوْمِ الدين} [al-Fātiḥa: 4]. The maṣdar may also be annexed to its agent, on the basis that the day is made a witness against them, either literally or figuratively.

semin-durr:38-38.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {أَسْمِعْ بِهِمْ وَأَبْصِرْ}: In form this is an imperative, and in meaning it is an expression of wonder. The soundest of the i'rab analyses of it, as established in the science of grammar, is that its fāʿil (agent) is the noun governed by the preposition bā', and that the bā' is redundant (zāʾida), its redundancy being obligatory to set the wording right, because with the imperative form أَفْعِلْ the agent can only be a latent (mustatir) pronoun. It is not permissible to omit this bā' except before أَنْ and أَنَّ, as in his saying:
323 - 9- تَرَدَّدَ فيعا ضَوْءَها وشُعاعُها ... فَاَحْصِنْ وأَزْيِنْ لامرِئٍ أن تَسَرْبَلا
(This verse is quoted as printed in the source; its text appears corrupt.) That is, بِأَنْ تَسَرْبَلَ ("that he be clothed"): the prepositional phrase is thus in the position of the nominative, and there is no pronoun in أَفْعَلِ. We have a second view: that the agent is a pronoun, and what is meant by it is the speaker, as though the speaker were commanding himself to do so, and the prepositional phrase after it is in the position of the accusative; this is ascribed to al-Zajjāj.
We have a third view: that the agent is a pronoun referring to the maṣdar (verbal noun), and the prepositional phrase is likewise in the position of the accusative, the implied meaning being: "Be excellent, O excellence, in respect of Zayd!" Because the agent here resembles an optional complement (faḍla) in form, according to the majority, it may be omitted when it is indicated, as in this verse, whose implied form is: وَأَبْصِرْ بِهِمْ ("and see well through them"). There are further discussions of it, the place for which is the books of grammar.
His saying {يَوْمَ يَأْتُونَنَا} is governed by أَبْصِرْ. It cannot be governed by أَسْمِعْ, because one may not separate a verb of wonder from what it governs; for that reason the sound view is that the matter cannot be a case of tanāzuʿ (competition of two verbs for one object). Some have allowed it while insisting on giving effect to the second verb, which is contrary to the rule of ʿamal (government). It has also been said that it is truly an imperative, and the one commanded is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, the meaning being: "Make the people hear and see them, through them and through their report, what will be done to them of punishment." This is transmitted from Abū l-ʿĀliya.
His word "اليوم" ("today") is accusative through what the preposition in his saying "في ضلال مبين" implies, that is: "but the wrongdoers are settled in manifest error today". It is not permissible for this adverbial to be the khabar (predicate) with the prepositional phrase being idle (laghw), so that a time would not be predicated of a physical body; by contrast with your saying "the fighting is today in Zayd's house", where both analyses are permissible.

semin-durr:39-39.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {إِذْ قُضِيَ الأمر}: It may be accusative through الحسرة ("the regret"), since a maṣdar (verbal noun) made definite by al- governs a direct object according to some, so how much more an adverbial? It may also be a badal (substitute) for "يوم", and so be governed by "أَنْذر" ("warn"). Thus said Abū l-Baqāʾ and al-Zamakhsharī, and the Shaykh followed them, mentioning only the badal.
This is not permissible if the adverbial remains in its true sense, since it is impossible for the future to govern the past. If you make "اليوم" a mafʿūl bihi (direct object), meaning "make them fear the day itself", that is, they fear the very day, that is sound, because the adverbial has passed over into the category of true objects.
His saying: {لكن الظالمون} is an instance of putting the overt noun in the place of the pronoun.
His saying: {وَهُمْ فِي غَفْلَةٍ وَهُمْ لاَ يُؤْمِنُونَ}: two ḥāl (circumstantial) clauses, with two views about them. The first: they are two ḥāl from the latent pronoun in his saying {فِي ضَلاَلٍ مُّبِينٍ}, that is: "they are settled in manifest error in these two evil states". The second: they are two ḥāl from the object of "أَنْذِرْهُم", that is: "warn them in this state and what follows". On the first view his saying {وَأَنْذِرْهُم} is a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ).

semin-durr:40-40.t: The majority read "يُرْجَعون" with yā' (with two dots below), as a passive. Al-Sulamī, Ibn Abī Isḥāq and ʿĪsā read it as an active. Al-Aʿraj read it with tā' (with two dots above) as a passive in the second person, which may or may not be an iltifāt (shift of person).

semin-durr:42-42.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {إِذْ قَالَ لأًبِيهِ}: It may be a badal ishtimāl (substitute of inclusion) for "إبراهيم", as was said earlier on {إِذِ انتبذت} [Maryam: 16]. On this view he has separated the substitute from that which it substitutes for by his saying: {إِنَّهُ كَانَ صِدِّيقاً نَّبِيّاً}, as in: "I saw Zayd - and what an excellent man! - your brother." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It is also possible that 'إذ' is attached to 'كان' or to 'صِدِّيقاً نبيَّاً', that is: he combined the qualities of the truthful and the prophets when he addressed his father with those addresses." For that reason Abū l-Baqāʾ allowed {صِدِّيقاً نبيَّاً} or its meaning to govern it.
The Shaykh said: "The first analysis, that is, the badal, requires 'إذ' to be inflected (tataṣarrafu), and it is not inflected. The second involves 'كان' governing an adverbial, on which there is a disagreement. The third requires that the governing element not be composed of the two words together, but that the government be attributed to one single word. Nor is it permissible for it to be governed by 'صِدِّيقاً', because it has been qualified by an adjective, except according to the Kufans. It is unlikely that it is governed by 'نبيَّاً', because that would imply that the prophethood was at the time of this speech."
I say: the governing element in it is what Abū l-Qāsim summarised and arranged with his fine craft from the two words together, as you saw in his words "that is: he combined / the qualities of the truthful and the prophets when he addressed his father".

semin-durr:43-43.t: The reading of Ibn ʿĀmir "يا أبَتِ" has already been given. In the codex (muṣḥaf) of ʿAbdallāh it is "وا أبتِ", with the "وا" of lamentation (nudba).

semin-durr:46-46.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {أَرَاغِبٌ أَنتَ}: Two analyses are possible. First: "راغبٌ" is a mubtadaʾ (subject) because it relies on the interrogative hamza, and "أنت" is a fāʿil (agent) that takes the place of the khabar (predicate). Second: it is a fronted khabar, and "أنت" is a postponed mubtadaʾ. The first is preferred for two reasons. One: it involves no fronting or postponing, since the rank of the fāʿil is to follow its governing word. Two: it does not require a separation between the governing word and what it governs by something not governed by that governing word; for {عَنْ آلِهَتِي} is attached to "راغِبٌ", so if "أنت" is made the agent, the separation is by what is like a part of the governing word, whereas if it is made the khabar it is an outsider, since it is not governed by "راغبٌ".
His saying: "مَلِيَّاً" has three accusative analyses. First: it is accusative as an adverbial of time, that is "for a long time", and from this come "المَلَوان" for night and day, and "مَلاوةُ الدَّهْر" (the long stretch of time), with the mīm vowelled in all three ways. He said:
324 - 0- فَعُسْنا بها من الشَّبابِ مَلاوةً ... فالحجُّ آيات الرسولِ المحبِّبِ
(We lived in it a long span of youth ... and the pilgrimage is the signs of the beloved Messenger.) Al-Suddī cited in support of this, from Muhalhil:
324 - 1- فتصَدَّعَتْ صُمُّ الجِبالِ لمَوْتِه ... وبَكَتْ عليه المُرْمِلاتُ مَلِيَّا
(The solid mountains split at his death, and the destitute women wept for him a long while.)
Second: it is accusative as a ḥāl, meaning "safe and sound". So Ibn ʿAbbās interpreted it, and it is a ḥāl from the agent of "اهْجُرْني". Ibn ʿAṭiyya likewise interpreted it, saying: "Its meaning is: independent, that is, well-off, from their saying 'he is malī' in such-and-such a thing." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "that is: capable." Third: it is an adjective of an omitted maṣdar, that is "a long abandonment" (هَجْراً مَلِيَّاً), meaning one broad and protracted, like the stretch of extended time.

semin-durr:47-47.t: Abū l-Burhasam read "سَلاماً" in the accusative; its explanation is clear from what has gone before.

semin-durr:49-49.t: His saying, the Exalted: {وَكُلاًّ جَعَلْنَا نَبِيّاً}: "وكُلاًّ" is a fronted mafʿūl (object), the first one, and "نبيَّا" is the second.

semin-durr:52-52.t: His saying, the Exalted: {نَجِيّاً}: a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the object of "قَرَّبْناه". Its original form is نَجِيْوٌ, because it is from نجا يَنْجو. As for "الأَيْمَن", the apparent view is that it is an adjective of "جانب", as shown by its following it in the saying of the Exalted: {وَوَاعَدْنَاكُمْ جَانِبَ الطور الأيمن} [Ṭāhā: 80]. It has also been said that it is an adjective of "الطور", since it derives from اليُمْن (blessing) and barakah.

semin-durr:53-53.t: His saying, the Exalted: {مِن رَّحْمَتِنَآ}: There are two analyses of this "مِنْ". One: it is causal, that is "because of our mercy". On this view "أخاه" is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object), "هرون" is a badal or ʿaṭf bayān (explicative apposition), or accusative with an implied "أَعْني" ("I mean"), and "نَبِيَّاً" is a ḥāl. Two: it is partitive, that is "part of our mercy". Al-Zamakhsharī said: "On this view 'أخاه' is a badal, and 'هرونَ' is ʿaṭf bayān." The Shaykh said: "The apparent view is that 'أخاه' is the object of 'وَهَبْنَا'; and 'مِنْ' is not a synonym of 'part' so that 'أخاه' could be a substitute for it."

semin-durr:55-55.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {مَرْضِيّاً}: The majority read it thus, with the weak letter altered. Its original form is مَرْضُوْوٌ, with two wāws, the first being the added one as in مَضْروب, and the second the lām of the word (the third radical), since it is from الرِّضْوان. It underwent ʿilāl (weak-letter change): the wāw was turned into yā' and the last was assimilated into a yā'; then the yā' and the wāw came together, the wāw was turned into yā' and assimilated. It is also permissible to pronounce the original form. This was dealt with earlier. Ibn Abī ʿAbla read it in this original form, which is the more frequent. An example of the ʿilāl is his saying:
324 - 2- لقد عَلِمَتْ عِرْسِي مُلَيْكَةُ أنني ... أنا المَرْءُ مَعْدِيَّاً عليه وعادِيا
(My wife Mulayka knows that I am the man who is attacked and who attacks.) They also said: أَرْضٌ مَسْنِيَّةٌ and مَسْنُوَّة, that is, "land watered by the sāniya (well-camel)".

semin-durr:58-58.t:
His saying: {مِّنَ النبيين مِن ذُرِّيَّةِ}: The first "مِن" is explicative (bayān), because all the prophets were favoured, so a partitive sense is impossible; the second is partitive, so its genitive noun is a badal (substitute) for what precedes it with repetition of the governing particle, a badal baʿḍ min kull (part for whole).
His saying: "وإسرائيلَ" is conjoined to "إبراهيمَ".
His saying: {وَمِمَّنْ هَدَيْنَا} may be conjoined to {مِّنَ النبيين}, and may be conjoined to {مِن ذُرِّيَّةِءَادَمَ}.
His saying: {إِذَا تتلى} is a conditional clause with two views. The more apparent: it has no grammatical position, being resumptive. The second: it is the khabar of "أولئك", and the relative noun before it is an adjective of the demonstrative; on the first view the relative noun itself is the khabar. The majority read "تُتلى" with two tā's (dots above). ʿAbdallāh, Shayba, Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀmir and Warsh from Nāfiʿ, in anomalous transmissions, read it with yā' (dots below) at the start; the feminine is figurative (majāzī), hence both forms occur in the verb.
His saying: "سُجَّدا" is an anticipated ḥāl (ḥāl muqaddara). Al-Zajjāj said: "because at the time of falling down they are not yet prostrating."
As for "بُكِيَّا", there are two views. The more apparent: it is the plural of باكٍ, though this is not the regular form; the regular plural is on the pattern فُعَلة, like قاضٍ and قُضاة, but this original form was not heard for it.
