It has already been mentioned that the two brothers (Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī) vocalise its first letter with kasra by assimilation to the vowel that follows (ittbāʿ). The second: it is a maṣdar on the pattern فُعُوْل, like جَلَسَ جُلُوْساً and قَعَدَ قُعوداً. On both views the original is بُكُوْي, with wāw and yā', and it underwent the well-known ʿilāl (weak-letter change) as in similar words. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "'وبكيَّا' with kasra on the [bā'] is a maṣdar and admits nothing else." The Shaykh said: "That is not right; rather ittbāʿ is permissible in it, and it is a plural like their saying عُصِيّ and دُليّ, plurals of عَصا and دَلْو." On this view "بكيَّاً" is either a maṣdar of corroboration for an omitted verb, that is "وبَكَوْا بُكِيَّاً", meaning "weeping"; or a maṣdar standing in the place of the ḥāl, that is "weeping" or "possessed of weeping"; or they are made [the very] weeping, as an exaggeration.

semin-durr:60-60.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {إِلاَّ مَن تَابَ وَآمَنَ}: There are two views. The more apparent: it is a connected exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil). Al-Zajjāj said: "It is disconnected (munqaṭiʿ)", and this is built on his view that the one who neglects the prayer is among the disbelievers.
ʿAbdallāh, al-Ḥasan, al-Daḥḥāk and a group read "الصلوات" in the plural. "الغَيُّ" has been treated earlier.
Al-Ḥasan read here, and everywhere in the Qur'an, "يُدْخَلون" as a passive. Al-Akhfash transmitted that it was read "يُلَقَّوْن", with ḍamma on the yā', fatḥa on the lām and shadda on the qāf, from لقَّاه in the intensive form. This reading will come, for some of the Seven, at the end of al-Furqān. "شيئاً" is either a maṣdar, that is "any wrong at all", or a direct object.

semin-durr:61-61.t:
His saying, the Exalted: {جَنَّاتِ عَدْنٍ}: The majority read it with kasra on the tā', accusative, as a badal (substitute) for "الجنةَ". On this reading his saying {وَلاَ يُظْلَمُونَ شَيْئاً} has two analyses. One: it is a parenthetical clause between the substitute and that for which it substitutes. Two: it is a ḥāl; so said the Shaykh. There is room for objection in this, in that an imperfect negated by "لا" is like an affirmative one in that the ḥāl-wāw cannot be attached directly to it.
Abū Ḥaywa, al-Ḥasan, ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and al-Aʿmash read "جناتُ" in the nominative, with two analyses. One: it is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, whose implied form is "those" or "it is the gardens of Eden". Two, which al-Zamakhsharī held: it is a mubtadaʾ, meaning that its khabar is {التي وَعَدَ}.
Al-Ḥasan ibn Ḥayy, ʿAlī ibn Ṣāliḥ and al-Aʿmash in one transmission read "جَنَّةَ عَدْنٍ" accusative, singular. Al-Yamānī, al-Ḥasan and al-Azraq from Ḥamza read "جنةُ" nominative singular; its explanation is clear from what has gone before. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Since it comprises the gardens of Eden, it was made a substitute for it, as you say: 'I saw your house, the courtyard and the upper rooms.' 'عَدْنٍ' is definite, a proper name (ʿalam) in the sense of العَدْن, which is residence, just as they made فينة, سحَر and أمس - for whoever does not make the last inflected - proper names for the meanings of 'the while', 'the daybreak' and 'yesterday'; so it was treated like العَدْن for that reason. Or it is a proper name for the land of Paradise because it is a dwelling place. Were it not so, the substitution would not be permissible, because an indefinite noun is not substituted for a definite one unless qualified, and describing it with 'التي' would not be permissible."
The Shaykh said: "What he mentioned is open to objection. As for his claim that عَدْناً is a proper name for the meaning of العَدْن, it needs textual authority and a hearing from the Arabs, and likewise his claim of its being a personal proper name. As for his saying 'Were it not so' up to 'unless qualified', that is not the school of the Basrans, for their school permits substituting an indefinite for a definite even if not qualified; this was said only by the Baghdadis, who are refuted by the attested usage as we have shown, and his entailment is invalid. As for his saying 'describing it with التي would not be permissible', it is not necessary that 'التي' be an adjective, and we have mentioned that it may be parsed as a badal."
I say: the apparent view is that "التي" is an adjective, and holding to this apparent view is sufficient. Moreover the relative noun is equivalent to derived nouns, and they have stated explicitly that substitution with a derived noun is weak, so too what is equivalent to it.
His saying: "بالغيبِ" has two analyses. One: the bā' is circumstantial (ḥāliyya). There are two possibilities for the owner of the ḥāl. One: the pronoun of "the Garden", returning to the relative noun, that is: "He promised it while it is absent from them, they do not see it". The other: it is from "عبادَه", that is: "while they are absent from it, not seeing it; they believed merely on the strength of His report".
The second analysis: the bā' is causal, that is: by reason of believing in the unseen and by reason of faith in it.
His saying: "إنه كان": two analyses are possible for this pronoun. One: it is the pronoun of the Creator, the Exalted, returning to "الرحمن", that is: "the Merciful, His promise was to be fulfilled". The other: it is the pronoun of the matter and affair (ḍamīr al-amr wa-l-shaʾn), because this is a place of exaltation and magnification. On the first view, "كان" may contain a pronoun that is its ism (subject) returning to Allah the Exalted, with "وعدُه" a badal ishtimāl for that pronoun and "مَأْتِيَّاً" its khabar. It is also possible that there is no pronoun in it, but that it takes "وَعْدُه" as its subject with "مَأْتِيَّاً" also its khabar, like: "Zayd's father was departing."
As for "مَأْتِيَّاً", there are two analyses. One: it is a passive participle in its normal sense, and what is meant by "the promise" is Paradise, the maṣdar being applied to it, that is, "that which is promised", like "a dirham is the Emir's striking" (i.e. a dirham struck by the Emir). It has also been said: "الوَعْدُ" is a maṣdar in its normal sense and "مَأْتِيَّاً" is a passive form with the sense of an active. Al-Zamakhsharī did not accept this; he said: "It has been said that 'مَأْتِيَّاً' is a passive with the sense of an active. The better view is that the promise is Paradise, and they come to it; or it is from your saying 'he brought good to him', that is: His promise was something done, fulfilled."

semin-durr:62-62.t:
His saying: {إِلاَّ سَلاَماً}: Al-Zamakhsharī put forward three analyses. One: its meaning is "if the greeting of some of them to others, or the angels' greeting to them, is idle talk, then they hear no idle talk beyond that"; so it belongs to the same vein as his saying:
323 - 4- ولا عيبَ فيهم غيرَ أنَّ سيوفَهم ... بهنَّ فُلولٌ من قراعِ الكتائبِ
(There is no fault in them except that their swords are notched from battering the regiments.)
Two: they hear nothing in it except speech in which they are safe from fault and deficiency, as a disconnected exception. Three: the meaning of "salām" is the prayer for safety; the abode of peace is the abode of safety, and its people need no prayer for safety, so its apparent sense would belong to idle talk and surplus speech were it not for the benefit of honouring that it contains.
I say: the apparent sense of this is that the exception on the first and last is connected, since he stated explicitly that it is disconnected in the second. As for the connectedness of the third, it is clear, because he applied "idle talk" to the greeting on the basis he mentioned. As for connectedness in the first, it is difficult, since that is not counted a fault, so it is not of the same kind as the first; the investigation of this will come, God willing, at the saying of the Exalted {لاَ يَذُوقُونَ فِيهَا الموت إِلاَّ الموتة الأولى} [al-Dukhān: 56].

semin-durr:63-63.t: His saying: {نُورِثُ}: Al-Aʿmash read "نُورِثها", bringing out the pronoun that refers back to the relative noun. Al-Ḥasan, al-Aʿraj and Qatāda read "نُوَرِّثُ" with fatḥa on the wāw and shadda on the rā', from "وَرَّثَ" in the intensive form.

semin-durr:64-64.t:
His saying: {وَمَا نَتَنَزَّلُ}: Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The wāw conjoins one sentence of speech to another, linking the two sayings even if their meaning is not the same." Al-Naqqāsh was strange in relating a view, namely that {وَمَا نَتَنَزَّلُ} is connected with His saying {قَالَ إِنَّمَآ أَنَاْ رَسُولُ رَبِّكِ لأَهَبَ لَكِ} [Maryam: 19]. Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "'وما نَتَنَزَّل', that is: 'and the angels say'", making it governed by an implied "say". It has also been said that it is the speech of the people of Paradise, which is closer than the one before it.
"نَتَنَزَّل" is the mutual (muṭāwiʿ) form of "نَزَّل" with shadda, and implies action over a period of time, though it may not imply it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Tanazzul has two senses: descending gradually, and descending in general, as in his saying:
324 - 4- فَلَسْتُ لإِنسيٍّ ولكنْ لِمَلأَكٍ ... تَنَزَّلَ مِنْ جوِّ السَّماءِ يصوبُ
(I am not for a human but for an angel who descended from the atmosphere of the sky, coming down.)
because it is the muṭāwiʿ of نَزَّل, and نزَّل may mean أَنْزَلَ, and may mean doing it by degrees. What suits this place is the gradual descent, and the meaning is: our descent is at intervals, from time to time." I say: it has already been mentioned that he distinguishes between نزَّل and أنزل at the beginning of this passage.
The majority read "نَتَنَزَّل" with the nūn of the plural. Al-Aʿraj read "يَتَنزَّل" with the yā' of the third person. As to the agent then there are two views. One: it is the pronoun of Gabriel. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "His saying 'له ما بين أيدينا وما خَلْفَنَا' refutes it, because it is consistent with the plural. It is appropriate only as a statement about Gabriel that the Qur'an is not sent down except by Allah's command at the times He decrees." One may answer what Ibn ʿAṭiyya said by saying that it is on an implied "saying": that is, "saying: 'To Him belongs what is before us'".
Two: it returns to the revelation (waḥy); so too said al-Zamakhsharī, as a report from Gabriel, with the pronoun being for the revelation, and this "saying" which I mentioned must also be implied.
His saying: {لَهُ مَا بَيْنَ أَيْدِينَا}: Some grammarians took this verse as proof that the tenses are three: past, present and future. It is like the saying of Zuhayr:
324 - 5- وأعلمُ عِلْمَ اليومِ والأمسِ قبلَه ... ولكنني عن عِلْمِ ما في غَدٍ عَمِ
(I know the knowledge of today and of yesterday before it, but I am blind to the knowledge of what is in tomorrow.)

semin-durr:65-65.t:
His saying: {رَّبُّ السماوات}: three views. One: it is a badal (substitute) for "ربُّك". Two: it is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, that is "He is the Lord of". Three: it is a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is the imperative sentence after it; this goes along with the view of al-Akhfash, who permits the fā' to be added in the khabar of a mubtadaʾ without restriction.
His saying "لعبادتِه" is attached to "اصْطَبِرْ". Its due would have been to be made transitive with "عَلَى", because that is its complement, as in His saying {واصطبر عَلَيْهَا} [Ṭāhā: 132]; but it has been given the sense of steadfastness, because worship has burdens which few remain steadfast in, so it is as if it were said: "be steadfast in it, enduring patiently."
His saying "هل تعلم": the two brothers (Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī), Hishām and a group assimilated the lām of "هل" into the tā'. They cited in support the verse of Muzāḥim al-ʿUqaylī:
324 - 6- فدَعْ ذا ولكن هَتُّعِيْنُ مُتَيَّماً ... على ضوءِ بَرْقٍ آخرَ الليلِ ناصِبِ
(Leave this; but will you help a love-struck man by the light of a flash of lightning at the end of the night, which is bright?) [Translator's note: the printed text reads "هَتُّعِيْنُ", apparently هل تعين, assimilated.]

semin-durr:66-66.t:
His saying: {أَإِذَا مَا مِتُّ}: "إذا" is accusative through an implied verb indicated by His saying {لَسَوْفَ أُخْرَجُ}, whose implied form is: "when I die, am I to be raised, or brought to life". It is not permissible that the governing word in it be "أُخْرَج", because what follows the lām of ibtidāʾ (the emphatic lām) does not govern what precedes it. Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "because what follows the lām and 'sawfa' does not govern what precedes it, like inna." I say: he made the preventing factor the two particles together. As for the lām, that is granted; as for the particle of futurity, it has no role in the prevention, because what follows a futurity particle can govern what precedes it. You say: "زيداً سأضرب" and "سوف أضرب"; but there is a weak disagreement on it, and the correct view is permissibility, and they cited in support:
324 - 7- فلمَّا رَأَتْع أمُّنا هانَ وَجْدُها ... وقالت: أبونا هكذا سوف يَفْعَلُ
(When our mother saw it her grief eased, and she said: "Our father will do just so.") [Translator's note: the printed text reads "رَأَتْع", apparently رأته.] Here "هكذا" is accusative through "يَفْعَل" after the futurity particle.
Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: The lām in His saying "لَسَوْف" is brought in to relate speech that came before with this meaning, as if someone said to the disbeliever: "When you die, so-and-so, you will surely be brought out alive", and he repeated the speech upon speech by way of finding it improbable, and repeated the lām to relate the first statement.
The Shaykh said: "This implied sense is not needed, nor that this is a report of speech that came before; rather it is the speech of the disbeliever, and it is a question that has the sense of denial and finding improbable."
Al-Zamakhsharī said: "The lām of ibtidāʾ entering on the imperfect gives the sense of the present, so how did it combine with the particle of the future? I say: it did not combine with it except as made purely for emphasis, as the hamza in 'يا الله' is made purely for compensation, and the sense of definiteness fades from it." The Shaykh said: "What he mentioned, that the lām gives the present, is disputed; so on the view of one who does not hold that, the question falls away. As for his saying 'as the hamza was made pure', that holds only on the view of one who claims that its origin is إلاه; as for one who claims its origin is لاه, the hamza in it is not for compensation, since nothing was dropped from it. And were we to say that its origin is إلاه and the first letter of the word was dropped, it would not follow that the hamza in the vocative is for compensation, since if it were compensation for what was dropped, it would be permanent in the vocative and elsewhere, and its omission in the vocative would not be allowed; yet they say 'يا الله' with it omitted, and they have stated explicitly that [pronouncing] the hamzat al-waṣl in the vocative is anomalous."
The majority read "أإذا" with the interrogative, and it is an expression of finding it improbable, as already said. Ibn Dhakwān, with a disagreement about him, and a group read "إذا" with a single hamza as a statement, or as an interrogative with its particle omitted because it is known, and because the other reading indicates it.
Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif read "لَسَأَخْرَجُ" with the sīn without sawfa; this is al-Zamakhsharī's report from him, while others reported from him "سَأَخْرُج" without the lām of ibtidāʾ, and on this reading the governing word of the adverbial is "أُخْرَج" itself, and the particle of futurity does not prevent it, on the correct view.
The majority read "أُخْرَجُ" as a passive. Al-Ḥasan and Abū Ḥaywa read "أَخْرِجُ" as an active. "حَيَّاً" is a corroborating ḥāl, because it is inherent in his coming out that he be "alive", like His saying {أُبْعَثُ حَيّاً} [Maryam: 33].
Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, ʿĀṣim and a group read "يَذْكُرُ" lightened, the imperfect of "ذكر"; the others read it with shadda, the imperfect of تَذَكَّر, the original being "يتذكَّر", the tā' being assimilated into the dhāl. Ubayy read it in this original form, "يَتَذَكَّر".

semin-durr:67-67.t:
The hamza in His saying {أَوَلاَ يَذْكُرُ} is, in implied order, postponed after the conjunction, as is the view of the majority. Al-Zamakhsharī returned here to the view of the majority, saying: "The wāw conjoins {لاَ يَذْكُرُ} to 'يقول', and the hamza of denial was placed between the conjoined and the conjunction." His own school is to posit, between the conjunction and the interrogative hamza, a sentence to which what follows is conjoined; and he did this - I mean returning to the view of the majority - in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf, as I pointed out in its place.
His saying: {مِن قَبْلُ}, that is: before his being raised. Al-Zamakhsharī interpreted it: "before the state he is in, which is the state of his existing."

semin-durr:68-68.t:
His saying: {جِثِيّاً}: an anticipated ḥāl (ḥāl muqaddara) from the object of "لَنُحْضِرَنَّهُمْ". "جِثِيّاً" is the plural of جاثٍ, a plural on the pattern فُعُوْل, like قاعِد, قُعود and جالِس, جُلوس. Its lām (third radical) has two dialects: one wāw, the other yā'. One says جثا يَجْثُو جُثُوَّاً and جَثِيَ يَجْثِي جِثايةً. On the first supposition its original is "جُثُوْوٌ" with two wāws, the first being added as the mark of the plural and the second the lām of the word; then it underwent ʿilāl like عِصِيّ and دُلِيّ, and the investigation of this came earlier under "عِتِيَّاً". On the second, the original is جُثُوْياً, and it underwent ʿilāl like هَيِّن and مَيِّت. From Ibn ʿAbbās: it has the sense of "groups upon groups", as the plural of جُثْوَة, which is what is heaped up of earth and stones. Its soundness from him is open to question, in that فُعْلَة is not pluralised on فُعُوْل. It is also possible that "جِثِيَّا" is a maṣdar on فُعول, and its original, as already stated for when it is a plural, is either جُثُوٌّ or جُثُوْيٌ.
It has already been mentioned that the two brothers (Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī) vocalise its first letter with kasra, and the rest with ḍamma.
"الجُثُوُّ" is sitting on the knees.

semin-durr:69-69.t:
His saying: {أَيُّهُمْ أَشَدُّ}: There are many views on this verse. The most apparent, according to the majority of the parsers and the school of Sībawayh, is that "أيُّهم" is a relative with the sense of "الذي", that its vowel is a vowel of indeclinability (binā'), made indeclinable according to Sībawayh because it departs from its peers; "أَشَدُّ" is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ; the sentence is the ṣila (relative clause) of "أيُّهم"; and "أيُّهم" with its ṣila is in the position of the accusative, as object of "لَنَنْزِعَنَّ".
"أيّ" has four states. One in which it is made indeclinable is, as in the verse, when it is annexed and the beginning of its ṣila is omitted. Like it is the saying of the poet:
324 - 8- إذا ما أَتَيْتَ بني مالكٍ ... فَسَلِّمْ على أيُّهم أَفْضَلُ
(When you come to the Banū Mālik, greet whichever of them is best.)
with ḍamma on "أيُّهم"; its details are settled in the topics of grammar.
Al-Khalīl, may Allah have mercy on him, claimed that "أيُّهم" here is a mubtadaʾ and "أشدُّ" its khabar, that it is interrogative, and that the sentence is quoted after an implied saying, the implied form being: "We shall pluck out of every party those of whom it is said: which of them is strongest?" Al-Khalīl strengthened his analysis with the saying of the poet:
324 - 9- ولقد أَبَيْتُ من الفتاةِ بمنزلٍ ... فَأَبَيْتُ لا حَرِجٌ ولا مَحْرُوْمُ
(I have spent the night with the girl in a dwelling, and I spent the night "neither constrained nor deprived".)
He said its implied form is: "I spent the night, it being said of me: 'neither constrained nor deprived'."
Yūnus held that it is interrogative and an initial mubtadaʾ, with what follows as its khabar, like the view of al-Khalīl, except that he claimed it is suspended (muʿallaqa) from "نَنْزِعَنَّ", so it is in the position of the accusative, because he allows suspension with all verbs and does not restrict it to verbs of the heart as the majority do.
Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It is possible that the plucking falls on {مِن كُلِّ شِيعَةٍ}, as in {وَوَهَبْنَا لَهْمْ مِّن رَّحْمَتِنَا} [Maryam: 50], that is: 'We shall pluck out some of every party', as if someone said: 'Who are they?' and it was said: 'whichever of them is most insolent'." So he made "أيُّهم" a relative too, but in his view it is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, that is: "they are those who are the most severe".
The Shaykh said: "This is a laboured imposition of what is not needed, a claim of an omission that is not necessary, and making what appears to be one sentence into two."
Abū l-Baqāʾ related from al-Akhfash and al-Kisāʾī that the object of لَنَنْزِعَنَّ is {كُلِّ شِيعَةٍ} and "مِنْ" is added; he said: "Both allow the addition of 'مِنْ', and 'أيّ' is interrogative", that is: "We shall pluck out every party." This differs in meaning from the analysis of the majority, since theirs leads to partition, while this leads to generality, unless you make "مِنْ" mark the starting point and not partition, in which case the two analyses agree.
Al-Kisāʾī held that the meaning of "لننزِعَنَّ" is "لننادِيَنَّ" ("We shall call out"), so it was treated as that, and did not govern "أيّ". Al-Mahdawī said: "نادى is suspended when a sentence follows it, so it governs in meaning but not in wording."
Al-Mubarrad said: "'أيُّهم' is attached to 'شيعةٍ', and so is nominative, the meaning being: from those who formed parties - whichever of them is strongest, as though they were vying with each other in this."
On this view he must posit an omitted object for "نَنْزِعَنَّ". Some posited, in al-Mubarrad's statement: "from those who cooperated and then looked at which of them." Al-Naḥḥās said: "This is a good view, and al-Kisāʾī reported تَشايَعُوا with the sense of تعاونوا (cooperated)." I say: there is unease in this wording attributed to al-Mubarrad, and the one who transmitted from him did not make clear on what basis the nominative is, but Abū l-Baqāʾ made it clear, though he made "أيُّهم" the agent of the verbal sense contained in "شيعة"; he said: "The implied form is: 'We shall pluck out of every group that follows whichever of them', and it is on this view with the sense of 'الذي'."
It was transmitted from the Kufans that "أيُّهم" in the verse has the sense of a condition. The implied form: "whether their insolence is severe or not", as you say: "I struck the people, whichever of them was angry", the meaning being: "whether they were angry or not."
Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif, Muʿādh ibn Muslim al-Farrāʾ, the teacher of al-Farrāʾ, and Zāʾida from al-Aʿmash read "أيُّهم" in the accusative. I say: on this reading and the preceding one, the school of Sībawayh should be that both its inflection and its indeclinability are permissible, which is the well-known view among those who transmit from him, though it has also been transmitted from him that he insists on its indeclinability. Al-Naḥḥās said: "I know of none of the grammarians but that he declared Sībawayh mistaken." He said: "I heard Abū Isḥāq al-Zajjāj say: 'It has not become clear to me that Sībawayh erred in his book except in two places, and this is one of them.' He said: 'Sībawayh inflected "أيّاً" when it is single because it is annexed, so how does he make it indeclinable when annexed?'" Al-Jarmī said: "I left Basra and, from the time I left al-Khandaq until Mecca, I did not hear anyone say 'لأَضْرِبَنَّ أيُّهم قائمٌ' with ḍamma; they all put it in the accusative."
{عَلَى الرحمن} is attached to "أشدُّ", and "عِتِيَّاً" is accusative as tamyīz (specification), converted from the mubtadaʾ, since the implied form is: "whichever of them, his insolence is the more severe". There must be an omitted element that completes the sentence, the implied form being: "then We cast him into the punishment" or "then We begin with his punishment". Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you ask: what are 'على' and the bā' attached to? Attaching them to the two maṣdars is not possible." I say: they are for explanation, not for complementing, or they are attached to "أَفْعَل", that is: "their insolence is greater against the Merciful, and their burning more fitting for the Fire", like their saying: "He is harder on his opponent" and "He is more fitting for such-and-such."
I say: by "على" he means His saying "على الرحمن", and by the bā' His saying "بالذين هم". By his saying "the two maṣdars" he means "عِتيَّا" and "صِلِيَّاً". As to its not being possible, that is because the maṣdar is in the status of a relative, and what is governed by a relative does not precede it.
Some allowed "عِتِيَّاً" and "صِلِيَّاً" in this verse to be two maṣdars as stated before, and allowed them to be the plurals of عاتٍ and صالٍ, in which case their accusative is as ḥāl. On this view "على" and the bā' may be attached to them, because the objection mentioned falls away.

semin-durr:71-71.t:
His saying: {وَإِن مِّنكُمْ إِلاَّ}: There are two views on this wāw. One: it conjoins this sentence to what precedes it. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "{وَإِن مِّنكُمْ إِلاَّ وَارِدُهَا} is an oath, and the wāw implies it, and the saying of the Prophet ﷺ explains it: 'Whoever has three of his children die, the Fire will not touch him except for the fulfilment of the oath (taḥillat al-qasam).'" The Shaykh said: "He overlooked the saying of the grammarians that the oath cannot be dispensed with by the answer's being indicated by the meaning, except when the answer is with a lām or with 'إنْ'; and the answer here, by his claim, is with the negative 'إنْ', so omitting the oath is not permissible according to what they stated. His saying 'the wāw implies it' shows that for him it is the wāw of oath, and no grammarian holds that a wāw like this is a wāw of oath, because that would require omitting the genitive noun while retaining the preposition, which is not permitted except in poetry or rare speech on the condition that the attribute of the omitted stands in its place, as they interpreted in their saying 'نِعْمَ السيرُ على بئسَ العَيْرُ', that is: 'on a donkey, a bad donkey it is', and the verse of the poet:
325 - 0- واللهِ ما ليلى بنامِ صاحِبُهْ ...
that is, 'with a man whose companion sleeps'. This verse is not of that kind, since the sworn-by is not omitted with its attribute standing in its place."
"إنْ" is a particle of negation, and "منكم" is an attribute of an omitted noun, whose implied form is: "and none of you". The implied form may also be: "and there is none of you but one who is its comer". Parallels of this have come before.
The address in His saying "منكم" may or may not be an iltifāt (shift of person). Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It is a shift towards the human being, and the reading of Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿIkrima 'وإنْ منهم' supports it; or it is an address to the people without shifting to the one mentioned."
"الحَتْمُ" is decree and obligation. حَتَمَ means "made obligatory", [and حَتَمَه] "he decreed it", then "ḥatm" is applied to the thing decreed, as in the saying of the Exalted "هذا خَلْقُ الله" and "هذا دِرْهَمٌ ضَرْبُ الأميرِ". "على ربِّك" is attached to "حَتْم" because it has the sense of a passive participle, and for that reason He described it as "مَقْضِيَّاً".

semin-durr:72-72.t:
The majority read {ثُمَّ نُنَجِّيْ} with ḍamma on "ثُمَّ", as the conjunction. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ubayy, al-Jaḥdarī and Yaʿqūb read "ثَمَّ" with fatḥa, as the adverb of place, governed by what follows it, that is: "there We shall save those who were God-fearing."
The majority read "نُنَجِّيْ" with ḍamma on the first nūn, fatḥa on the second and shadda on the jīm, from "نجَّى" in the intensive form. Al-Kisāʾī, al-Aʿmash and Ibn Muḥayṣin read "نُنْجِي" from أَنْجى. On both, the verb is imperfect.
A group read "نُجِّيْ" with a single nūn with ḍamma and shadda on the jīm. On this reading it is a passive past, and its reader should have given fatḥa to the yā', but he made it sākin for lightness. This reading admits another explanation which will come in a mutawātir reading at the end of Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib also read "نُنَحِّي" with an undotted ḥā', from التَّنْحِيَة ("removing").
The object of "اتَّقوا" is omitted, being intended since it is known, that is: "they feared polytheism and wrongdoing".
His saying "جِثِيَّا" is either a second object if "نَذَرُ" takes two objects with the sense of "we leave" and "we make", or a ḥāl if you take "نَذَرُ" to mean "we leave them". "جِثِيَّاً" is as already stated.
"فيها" may be attached to "نَذَرُ", or to "جِثِيَّاً" if it is a ḥāl; that is not permissible if it is a maṣdar. It may also be attached to an omitted element as a ḥāl from "جِثِيَّاً", because it is originally an adjective of an indefinite noun that was put ahead of it and so became accusative as ḥāl.

semin-durr:73-73.t:
His saying: {مَّقَاماً}: Ibn Kathīr read "مُقاماً" with ḍamma, and it is transmitted from Abū ʿAmr, and it is the reading of Ibn Muḥayṣin. The others read with fatḥa. In both readings it may be a noun of place or a noun of the maṣdar, either from "قام" (triliteral) or from "أقام", that is: "the best place of standing or of residence".
"النَّدِيُّ" is on the pattern فَعِيل; its original is نَدِيْوٌ because its lām is a wāw. One says نَدَوْتُهم أَنْدَوْهم, that is "I came to their gathering place", and "النادي" is like it. From it is {فَلْيَدْعُ نَادِيَهُ} [al-ʿAlaq: 17], that is: the people of his gathering. "النَّدِيُّ" and "النادي" mean the people's assembly and their place of conversation. It is also said to be derived from النَّدى, which is generosity, because the generous gather in it; and انْتَدَيْتُ المكانَ and المُنْتدى are likewise. Ḥātim said:
325 - 1- ودُعِيْتُ في أَوْلَى النَّدِيَّ ولم ... يُنْظَرْ إليَّ بأَعْيُنٍ خُزْرِ
(I was called into the first of the assembly, and was not looked at with squinting eyes.)
The maṣdar is النَّدْوُ. "مَقاماً" and "نَدِيَّا" are accusative as tamyīz after the elative.
Abū Ḥaywa, al-Aʿraj and Ibn Muḥayṣin read "يُتْلَى" with yā' (dots below), and the others with tā' (dots above). The lām in "للذين" may be for conveying (lil-tablīgh), which is the apparent view, or for cause.

semin-durr:74-74.t:
His saying: {وَكَمْ أَهْلَكْنَا}: "كم" is a fronted object, whose fronting is obligatory because it has the head of the sentence, being either interrogative or predicative (khabariyya), the latter being carried over onto the interrogative. "أَهلَكْنا" acts upon "كم", that is: "many generations did We destroy". "مِنْ قَرنٍ" is a tamyīz of "كَمْ" explaining it.
His saying: {هُمْ أَحْسَنُ}: two views on this sentence. One, which al-Zamakhsharī and Abū l-Baqāʾ held: it is in the position of the accusative, an adjective of "كم". Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Do you not see that if you dropped 'هم' you would have to put 'أحسنُ' in the accusative as an adjective?" There is room for objection in this, because the grammarians stated that "كم", whether interrogative or predicative, is neither described nor used to describe. Two: it is in the position of the genitive as an adjective of "قَرْن", and there is no objection in that. "هم" was used in the plural only because "قَرْناً", though singular in wording, is plural in meaning; so "قَرْن" is like the word "جميع", and with "جميع" one may sometimes follow its wording and make it singular, as in His saying {نَحْنُ جَمِيعٌ مُّنتَصِرٌ} [al-Qamar: 44], and sometimes follow its meaning and pluralise what relates to it, as in His saying {لَّمَّا جَمِيعٌ لَّدَيْنَا مُحْضَرُونَ} [Yā Sīn: 32].
His saying "ورِئْياً": the majority read "رِئْياً" with a hamza with sukūn followed by a clear yā', in continuous reading and in pause. Ḥamza, when he pauses, turns this hamza into a yā', according to his principle of easing the hamza; then he has two options after that: to keep them distinct, having regard to the origin, or to assimilate, having regard to the pronunciation. In keeping them distinct there is a difficulty that is not hidden, and in assimilation there is a suggestion that it is another root, namely الرَّيّ, in the sense of fullness and freshness; for this reason Abū ʿAmr abandoned his principle of easing its hamza.
Qālūn from Nāfiʿ and Ibn Dhakwān from Ibn ʿĀmir read "ورِيَّا" with a doubled yā' after the rā'. It has been said: it is originally with hamza, and then the hamza was turned into a yā' and assimilated. "الرَّأْيُ" with hamza is said to be from seeing with the eye, with فِعْل in the sense of مَفْعول, that is "seen". It has also been said to be from الرُّواء and beauty of appearance. And it has been said: rather it is from الرَّيّ, the opposite of thirst, and is not hamzated originally, the meaning being "better in appearance", because quenched fullness is better than their two opposites.
Ḥumayd and Abū Bakr ibn ʿĀṣim, in al-Aʿshā's transmission, read "وَرِيْئاً" with a yā' with sukūn followed by a hamza. It is a transposition (maqlūb) of "رِئْياً" in the reading of the majority, and its pattern is فِلْعٌ, and it is from راءه يَرْآه, like the saying of the poet:
325 - 2- وكلُّ خليلٍ راءَني فهو قائلٌ ... مِنَ أجلِكَ: هذا هامةُ اليومِ أوغدِ
(Every friend who saw me says, because of you: "This one is the head of today, or of tomorrow.") [Translator's note: the second hemistich is printed thus and appears corrupt.]
And in transposition from transposition is what is in it.
Al-Yazīdī transmitted the reading "ورِياء" with a yā' followed by an alif followed by a hamza, from المُراءاة, that is: each of them shows the other's beauty; then the first hamza was eased by turning it into a yā', which is a regular easing.
Ibn ʿAbbās also read, in Ṭalḥa's transmission, "وَرِيَاً" with a single light yā'. It has two explanations. One: its origin is like Qālūn's reading, then the word was lightened by dropping one of the two yā's, the second, because the heaviness arose through it, and because it is the lām of the word, and final letters are more apt to change. Two: its origin is like Ḥumayd's reading "وَرِيْئا" with the transposition, then the vowel of the hamza was moved to the yā' before it and the hamza dropped by the rule of easing hamza by transfer, so it became "وَرِيا" as you see. Some people boldly made this reading a solecism (laḥn), and the one who errs is none other than he, because its explanation was hidden from him.
Ibn ʿAbbās also, and Ibn Jubayr and a group, read "وزِيَّا" with zāy and a doubled yā'. "الزَّيُّ" is fine apparel and gathered equipment, since it is from زَوَى كذا يَزْوِيه, that is "he gathers it", and the one who adorns himself gathers the things that adorn him and display his appearance.

semin-durr:75-75.t:
His saying: {مَن كَانَ فِي الضلالة}: "مَنْ" may be conditional, which is the apparent view, or a relative, with the fā' entering the khabar because the relative contains the sense of a condition. His saying "فَلْيَمْدُدْ" has two views. One: it is a request in its normal sense, meaning supplication. Two: its wording is that of the imperative and its meaning that of a statement. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "that is: the Merciful extends to him, in the sense of giving him respite; it came out in the form of the imperative to signal the necessity of that. Or 'let him be given respite' in the sense of a supplication that Allah give him respite and extend the span of his life."
His saying: "حتى إذا": for this "حتى" what has been said of its peers applies, that it is either a preposition or a particle of commencement; the matter lies only in that for which it marks the limit, on both views. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "There are two views in this verse: that it is connected with the verse which is the fourth after it, the two verses being parenthetical between them, that is: 'They said: Which of the two groups is better in standing and finer in assembly?' - until, when they see what they are promised; that is: they do not cease saying this saying and being fond of it, never desisting from it until they witness what was promised with their own eyes." And he mentioned fine words.
Then he said: "The second: it is connected with what comes directly after it, the meaning being that those in error are given respite", and he mentioned lengthy words. Then he said: "until they see with their eyes the help of / Allah to the believers, or witness the Hour and its preliminaries. If you ask: what is this 'ḥattā'? I say: it is the one after which sentences are quoted. Do you not see that the conditional sentence occurs after it: {إِذَا رَأَوْاْ مَا يُوعَدُونَ... فَسَيَعْلَمُونَ}?"
The Shaykh said, finding the first view very unlikely: "It is extremely far-fetched because of the length of the separation between His saying 'They said, which of the two groups' and the limit, and it involves separation by two parenthetical sentences, which Abū ʿAlī does not allow." This finding unlikely is near the mark. Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "'ḥattā' here introduces what follows it, and it is not attached to a verb."
His saying: {إِمَّا العذاب وَإِمَّا الساعة}: you know what there is in "إمَّا", as to whether it is a conjunction or not, and there is no disagreement that one of its meanings is division, as in the noble verse. "العذابَ" and "الساعةَ" are two badals for His saying {مَا يُوعَدُونَ}, which is accusative through "رَأَوْا", and "فَسَيَعْلمون" is the apodosis of the condition.
{مَنْ هُوَ شَرٌّ مَّكَاناً}: "مَنْ" may be a relative with the sense of "الذي", the object of "يَعْلَمون". It may also be interrogative, in the position of the nominative as mubtadaʾ, with "هو" a second mubtadaʾ and "شَرٌّ" its khabar, the mubtadaʾ and khabar being the khabar of the first. The sentence may also be suspended (muʿallaqa) from the verb of seeing, so the sentence is in the position of the accusative by suspension.

semin-durr:76-76.t:
His saying: {وَيَزِيدُ الله}: There are two views on this sentence. One: it has no grammatical position, being resumptive, since it was brought to report this. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It is conjoined to the position of 'فَلْيَمْدُدْ', because that stands in the place of the khabar, the implied form being: 'Whoever is in error, the Merciful extends - or will extend - to him, and increases.'" The Shaykh said: "It is not sound that 'ويَزيدُ' be conjoined to 'فَلْيَمْدُدْ', whether the latter is a supplication or a statement in the form of an imperative, since it is in the place of the khabar if 'مَنْ' is a relative, or in the place of the apodosis if 'مَنْ' is conditional; and on either supposition the sentence 'ويزيدُ اللهُ الذين اهتدَوا هدىً' lacks a pronoun returning to 'مَنْ' to link the khabar sentence with the mubtadaʾ, or the protasis with the apodosis which is 'فَلْيَمْدُدْ' and what is conjoined to it; because what is conjoined to a khabar is a khabar, and what is conjoined to the apodosis sentence is apodosis. And when the conditional particle is a noun, not an adverbial, it is necessary that the apodosis sentence contain its pronoun or what takes its place, and likewise the sentence conjoined to it."
I say: Abū l-Baqāʾ also mentioned as al-Zamakhsharī did. One may answer what the two said: on this supposition we choose that "مَنْ" be conditional. His saying "a pronoun returning to the conditional noun, other than an adverbial, is indispensable" is disputed, for there is a disagreement on it, whose investigation and the evidence for it I gave earlier in Sūrat al-Baqara. Al-Zamakhsharī and Abū l-Baqāʾ may be among those who say that it is not required.

semin-durr:77-77.t:
His saying: {أَفَرَأَيْتَ}: conjoined with the fā' to signal that it follows immediately, as if it were said: He also reported the story of this disbeliever right after the story of those. "أَرَأَيْتَ" has the sense of "tell me", as you know. The relative is the first object, and the second is the interrogative sentence of His saying {أَطَّلَعَ الغيب}. "لأُوْتَيَنَّ" is the answer to an implied oath, and the whole oath sentence is in the position of the accusative by "saying".
His saying here "وَوَلداً": and in it {قَالُواْ اتخذ الرحمن وَلَداً} [Maryam: 88, 91] are two places. In al-Zukhruf {إِن كَانَ للرحمن وَلَدٌ} [verse 81], and in Nūḥ {مَالُهُ وَوَلَدُهُ} [verse 21]. The two brothers (Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī) read the four with ḍamma on the wāw and sukūn on the lām. Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr agreed with them on the one in Nūḥ, not on the two sūras. The others, namely Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir and ʿĀṣim, read all of them with fatḥa on the wāw and the lām.
The reading with two fatḥas is clear: it is a singular noun standing in for the plural. As for the reading with ḍamma and sukūn, it is said to be like the preceding in meaning; one says وَلَد and وُلْد, as one says عَرَب and عُرْب, عَدَم and عُدْم. It has also been said: rather it is the plural of وَلَد, like أَسَد and أُسْد, and they recited in support of that:
325 - 3- ولقد رَأَيْتُ معاشراً ... قد ثَمَّروا مالاً وَوُلْدا
(I have seen groups who have multiplied wealth and offspring.) They also recited as evidence that الوَلَد and الوُلْد are synonyms the following:
325 - 4- فَلَيْتَ فلاناً كان في بَطْنِ أمِّه ... وليت فلاناً كان وُلْدَ حمارِ
(Would that so-and-so had been in his mother's belly, and would that so-and-so had been the offspring of a donkey.)
ʿAbdallāh and Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar read "ووِلْدا" with kasra on the wāw, a dialect form of الوَلَد, and it is not far-fetched that this belongs to the category of الذِّبْح and الرِّعْي, so that وِلْدٌ would mean مَوْلود (what is born); and likewise for the one with two fatḥas, like القَبَض meaning المَقْبوض.

semin-durr:78-78.t:
His saying: {أَطَّلَعَ}: This is the hamza of interrogation, because of which the hamzat al-waṣl fell. It has also been read with its dropping in continuous reading and its kasra at the start, the interrogative hamza having been omitted because "أم" indicates it, as in:
325 - 5- لَعَمْرُكَ ما أَدْري وإن كنتُ دارِيا ... بسَبْعٍ رَمَيْنَ الجَمْرَ أم بثمانِ
(By your life, I do not know, though I be one who knows, whether they threw the pebbles with seven or with eight.)
"واطَّلع" is from their saying: اطَّلَعَ فلانٌ الجبلَ, that is, he climbed to its top. Jarīr said:
325 - 6-. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... لا قَيْتُ مُطَّلَعَ الجِبالِ وُعُوْرا
(I met with the ascent of the mountains rugged.) [Translator's note: the first hemistich is elided in the source.] So "الغيبَ" is a direct object, not by omission of the preposition, that is "على الغيب", as some have claimed.

semin-durr:79-79.t:
His saying: {كَلاَّ}: The grammarians have six views on this word. One, the school of the majority of the Basrans such as al-Khalīl, Sībawayh, Abū l-Ḥasan al-Akhfash and Abū l-ʿAbbās: it is a particle of rebuke and deterrence, and this is a meaning fitting for it wherever it occurs in the Qur'an, and how fine it is here in this verse, where it rebukes and deters that speaker. Two, the school of al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl: it is a particle of affirmation with the sense of "yes" (naʿam), so it is an answer, and something must then precede it, in wording or implied; it may also be used in oaths. Three, the school of al-Kisāʾī, Abū Bakr ibn al-Anbārī, Naṣīr ibn Yūsuf and Ibn Wāṣil: it has the sense of "truly" (ḥaqqan). Four, the school of Abū ʿAbdallāh Muḥammad al-Bāhilī: it is a rejection of what precedes it, which is close to the meaning of deterrence. Five: it is an inserted filler in speech with the sense of "ī" (yes, by), so it was said. There is room for objection in this, since "ī" is a particle of response but restricted to oaths. Six: it is a particle of commencement, which is the view of Abū Ḥātim. For establishing these points there is a subject more fitting, in which I have investigated them, by the praise of Allah the Exalted.
It has also been read here with fatḥa and tanwīn on this "كَلاَّ", and this is transmitted from Abū Nuhayk. It will come that al-Zamakhsharī relates this reading and ascribes it to Ibn Nuhayk at His saying {كَلاَّ سَيَكْفُرُونَ} [Maryam: 82], and also relates a reading with ḍamma on the kāf and tanwīn, ascribing it likewise to Ibn Nuhayk. As for his saying "Ibn Nuhayk", they have no Ibn Nuhayk; they have only Abū Nuhayk, by kunya.
In the reading with fatḥa and tanwīn there are four views. One: it is accusative as a maṣdar of an implied verb of its own wording, whose implied form is "كَلُّوا كَلاًّ", that is, "they grew weary of the truth with weariness", or "they grew weary of worshipping Allah through their negligence of it", from the saying of the Arabs "the sword grew blunt" (كَلَّ السيفُ) when it fails to strike, and "Zayd grew weary" (كَلَّ زيد), that is, he tired. It is also said: the meaning is: they failed in their claim and were cut off. Two: it is a direct object of a verb implied from the meaning of the speech, whose implied form is "they bore a burden" (حَمَلُوا كَلاَّ); "الكَلُّ" is also a burden. You say "so-and-so is a burden (kall) on the people", and from it is His saying {وَهُوَ كَلٌّ على مَوْلاهُ} [al-Naḥl: 76]. Three: the tanwīn is a substitute for the alif of "كَلاَّ", which is intended as rebuke and deterrence, so it would also be inflected as a diptote-converted. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Someone may say: if this transmission is sound, it is the 'kallā' of deterrence, and the one pausing on it turned its alif into a nūn, as in {قَوَارِيرَاْ} [al-Insān: 15]." The Shaykh said: "This is not good, because he said 'the one of deterrence', and the one of deterrence is a particle, and there is no ground for turning its alif into a nūn. His likening it to 'قواريرا' is not good either, because 'قواريرا' is a noun returned to its original, so the tanwīn is not a substitute for an alif but the tanwīn of inflection (ṣarf); and this plural is disputed: is withholding its tanwīn obligatory or permitted? There are two views. It is also transmitted that the dialect of some Arabs inflects what is not normally inflected. So this view is either on the view of those who do not hold it obligatory or on that dialect."
Four: it is an adjective of "آلهة"; so said Ibn ʿAṭiyya. There is room for objection, since the meaning is not that. A ground may appear for him: that He described the gods by "الكَلّ", which is a maṣdar meaning exhaustion and incapacity, as if it were said: "gods that are weary", that is incapable and cut off; and when He described them by the maṣdar, He made it singular.

semin-durr:82-82.t:
Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Dānī and others transmitted from Abū Nuhayk that he read "كُلاَّ" with ḍamma on the kāf and tanwīn. There are two interpretations: one, that it is accusative as a ḥāl, that is "they will all disbelieve"; so Abū l-Baqāʾ implied it, and found it unlikely. Two: it is accusative through an implied verb, that is, "they will reject, or deny, or be abandoned, all of them"; so said Ibn ʿAṭiyya.
Ibn Jarīr related that Abū Nuhayk read "كُلٌّ" with ḍamma on the kāf and nominative with tanwīn on the lām, as a mubtadaʾ, with the verbal sentence after it as its khabar. The apparent wording of these scholars is that it was read thus only in the second "كُلاَّ".
ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib read "ونُمِدُّ" from أمَدَّ. The discussion of مَدَّه and أمدَّه has come earlier.
His saying: {وَنَرِثُهُ مَا يَقُولُ} [Maryam: 80]: two views are possible for "ما". One: it is a direct object, and the pronoun in "نَرِثُه" is accusative by omission of the preposition, the implied form being: "and We inherit from him what he says". Two: it is a badal ishtimāl for the pronoun in "نَرِثُه". Some posited a muḍāf before the relative, that is: "We inherit the meaning of what he says", or "the referent of what he says", which is the wealth and children, because the speech itself is not inherited.
"فَرْداً" is a ḥāl, either an anticipated one, like {فادخلوها خَالِدِينَ} [al-Zumar: 73], or a concurrent one, and that is built on a disagreement over the meaning of the verse mentioned in al-Kashshāf.
The pronoun in {سَيَكْفُرُونَ} may return to the gods because they are the nearest mentioned, and because the pronoun in "يكونون" also returns only to them. Like it: {وَإِذَا رَأى الذين أَشْرَكُواْ شُرَكَآءَهُمْ} [al-Naḥl: 86], then He said: {فَألْقَوْا إِلَيْهِمُ القول إِنَّكُمْ لَكَاذِبُونَ}. It has also been said that it returns to the polytheists, like His saying: {والله رَبِّنَا مَا كُنَّا مُشْرِكِينَ} [al-Anʿām: 23]. However, this lacks agreement among the pronouns, since the pronoun in "يكونون" returns to the gods; and "بعبادتهم" is a maṣdar annexed to its agent if the pronoun in "عبادتهم" returns to the polytheists who worship, or to its object if it returns to the gods.
His saying "ضِدَّاً": He made it singular, though it is a predicate of a plural, for one of two reasons: either because it is a maṣdar originally, and maṣdars are singular and masculine; or because it is a singular with the sense of a plural. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "'الضِّدُّ' is the helper, made singular as in 'they are one hand against all others', because of the agreement of their word and that they are like one thing through the intensity of their solidarity and concord. 'الضِّدُّ' is the helper and the help. One says 'from your adhdād', that is, your helpers." It is said: the helper is called ḍidd because he opposes whoever is hostile to you and contradicts him by your being helped against him. In the exegesis: the ḍidd here means enemies. It is also said: the counterpart. It is also said: affliction; and this one fits the meaning of the verse.

semin-durr:83-83.t: His saying: {أَزّاً}: a corroborating maṣdar; "الأَزُّ", "الأَزيز", "الهَزُّ" and "الاستفزاز" are, said al-Zamakhsharī, "sisters", meaning agitation and intense disturbance. "الأزُّ" also means loudness of sound, from which "أَزَّ المِرْجَلُ أَزَّاً" and "أَزِيْزاً", that is: it boiled and its boiling intensified until a sound was heard from it. In the ḥadīth: "It had an azīz", that is, the palm trunk when the Prophet ﷺ left it.

semin-durr:85-85.t:
His saying: {يَوْمَ نَحْشُرُ}: accusative through "سَيَكْفرون", or through {يَكُونُونَ عَلَيْهِمْ ضِدّاً}, or through "نَعُدُّ" which contains the sense of requital, or through His saying "لا يَمْلكون" which follows it, or through an implied verb, namely "اذْكُرْ" ("remember") or "احْذَرْ" ("beware"). It is also said to be governed by the answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "When will that be?" and it was said: "It will be on the day He gathers." And it is said that the implied form is: "On the day We gather and drive, We do to the two groups what description cannot encompass."
His saying "وَفْداً" is accusative as ḥāl, and likewise "وِرْداً". "الوَفْدُ" is the group of those who come as delegates. One says وَفَدَ يَفِدُ وَفْداً وَوُفُوداً ووِفادَةً, that is, he arrived by way of honour, so it is originally a maṣdar, then applied to persons like "ṣaff" (rank). Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "'وَفْدُ' is the plural of وافِد, like راكِب and رَكْب, صاحِب and صَحْب." What he said is not the school of Sībawayh, since a fāʿil is not pluralised on فَعْل according to Sībawayh. Al-Akhfash allowed it. As for رَكْبٌ and صَحْبٌ, they are collective nouns, not plurals, as shown by their diminutive on their own wording. He said:
325 - 7- أَخْشَى رُجَيْلاً ورُكَيْباً غادِيا ...
(I fear a little man and a little band of riders setting out in the morning.)
If you say: perhaps Abū l-Baqāʾ meant the lexical plural, the answer is that he said after his words "and 'الوِرْدُ' is a noun for the plural of وارِد", which shows that he meant the technical plural as opposed to the collective noun.

semin-durr:86-86.t:
"الوِرْدُ" is a noun for the group of thirsty ones coming to water, and it too is originally a maṣdar applied to persons. One says وَرَدَ الماءَ يَرِدُه وِرْداً ووُرُوْداً. The poet said:
325 - 8- رِدِي رِدي وِرْدَ قَطاةٍ صَمَّا ... كُدْرِيَّةٍ أَعٍجَبَها بَرْدُ المَا
(Come, come, as a deaf, dusky sandgrouse comes, delighted by the coolness of the water.)
Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "It is a noun for the plural of وارِد. It is also said: it has the sense of وارِد. It is also said: it is shortened from 'وارِد', which is far-fetched", meaning that it may be an adjective on the pattern فِعْل.
Al-Ḥasan and al-Jaḥdarī read "يُحْشَر المتقون، ويُساق المجرمون" in the passive.

semin-durr:87-87.t:
His saying: {لاَّ يَمْلِكُونَ}: two views on this sentence. One: it is resumptive, brought to report this. Two: it is in the position of the accusative as ḥāl from what has preceded. On this wāw there are two views. One: it is a mark of plurality, not a pronoun at all, but only a mark, as in the dialect "ate me the fleas" (akalūnī l-barāghīth), and the agent is "مِنْ اتَّخَذَ" since it has the sense of a plural; so said al-Zamakhsharī. There is remoteness in this, as if it were said: "None has power of intercession except those who have taken a covenant." The Shaykh said: "The Qur'an should not be taken to follow this rare dialect when it is clear that the wāw can be made a pronoun. Master Abū l-Ḥasan ibn ʿUṣfūr said: it is a weak dialect."
I say: they have said that of His saying {عَمُواْ وَصَمُّواْ كَثِيرٌ مِّنْهُمْ} [al-Māʾida: 71] and {وَأَسَرُّواْ النجوى الذين ظَلَمُواْ} [al-Anbiyāʾ: 3], so this place has a precedent in those two.
Then the Shaykh said: "Moreover, the alif, wāw and nūn that are marks and not pronouns are not known to be followed, as agent, by anything but an explicit plural, an explicit dual, or a conjunction. As for a singular word coming and being applied to a plural or dual, such a thing needs transmission to establish it. As for pronouns, dual or plural, returning to a word singular in form but intended as dual or plural, that is heard and well-known in the language of the Arabs; though it is possible to extend these marks by analogy to those pronouns, the safer course is to say it only on the basis of hearing."
Two: the wāw is a pronoun. Then there are four views on what it returns to. One: it returns to all creation, as the mention of the two groups - the God-fearing and the criminals - indicates them, since they are its two divisions. Two: it returns to the God-fearing and the criminals; and no difference from the first is apparent at all, because these two divisions are all creation. Three: it returns to the God-fearing only, or to the criminals only, which is arbitrary. His saying: {إِلاَّ مَنِ اتخذ}: this exception depends on what the wāw returns to. If it is said to return to creation, or to the two groups mentioned, or to the God-fearing only, then the exception is connected.
In the position of the excepted there are the two well-known views: either nominative as badal, or accusative as the original of exception. If it is said that it returns to the criminals only, it is a disconnected exception, and there are then the two well-known dialects: the Hijazi, obligatory accusative, and the Tamīmī, permitting it along with permitting badal as in the connected.
Al-Zamakhsharī made this exception from "الشفاعة", with an omitted muḍāf whose implied form is: "They have no power of intercession except the intercession of one who has taken", so its accusative is on the two views of badal and original exception, like "I saw no one except Zayd." Some said: the excepted-from is omitted and the implied form is: "They have no power of intercession for anyone except for one who has taken a covenant with the Merciful", the excepted-from being omitted because it is known, like the saying of another:
325 - 9- نجا سالمٌ والنفسُ منه بِشِدْقِهِ ... ولم يَنْجُ إلا جَفْنَ سَيْفٍ ومِئْزَرا
(Sālim escaped with his soul at his jaw, and nothing escaped but a sword scabbard and a waist wrapper.) That is: "and nothing escaped".
Ibn ʿAṭiyya made the exception connected even if the pronoun in {لاَّ يَمْلِكُونَ} returns to the criminals only, by taking "criminals" to mean the disbelievers and the disobedient among the Muslims. The Shaykh said: "Taking 'criminals' to mean the disbelievers and the disobedient is far-fetched." I say: there is no remoteness in it; and as he finds it far-fetched to apply "criminals" to the disobedient, so another finds far-fetched applying "God-fearing" to the disobedient; indeed applying "criminal" to the disobedient is better known than applying "God-fearing" to him.

semin-durr:89-89.t: His saying: {شَيْئاً إِدَّاً}: The majority read "إدَّاً" with kasra on the hamza, which is the great, abominable, astonishing matter. The Commander of the Faithful and al-Sulamī read it with fatḥa. They explained it by an omitted muḍāf, that is "شيئاً أدَّاً", because "الأدّ" with fatḥa is a maṣdar; one says أدَّه الأمرُ and أدَّني يَؤُدُّني أدَّاً, that is, "it weighed on me". The Shaykh had mentioned that الأَدّ and الإِدّ, with fatḥa and kasra on the hamza, mean wonder. It has also been said: it is the great abominable thing, and الإِدَّة is hardship. / On his statement that "الإِدّ and الأدّ have one meaning", there ought to be no need for an omitted muḍāf, unless he meant that they have the meaning of wonder in sense, not as to being a maṣdar or not.

semin-durr:90-90.t:
His saying: {تَكَادُ}: Nāfiʿ and al-Kisāʾī read it with yā' (dots below), and the others with tā' (dots above). Both are clear, since the feminine is figurative; likewise in Sūrat al-Shūrā.
Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim and Ḥamza read "يَنفَطِرْنَ", the imperfect of انْفَطَرَ. The others read "يتفطَّرْن", the imperfect of تَفَطَّرَ with shadda, in this sūra. As for the one in al-Shūrā, Ḥamza and Ibn ʿĀmir read it with tā' and yā' and shadda on the ṭā', and the others follow their principles for this sūra. The upshot is that Abū ʿAmr and Abū Bakr read with tā' and nūn in both sūras; that Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim read with tā' and yā' and shadda on the ṭā' in both; and that Ḥamza and Ibn ʿĀmir read with tā' and nūn in this sūra, and with tā' and yā' and shadda on the ṭā' in al-Shūrā.
"الانفِطارُ" is from "فَطَرَه" when he split it, and "التفطُّر" from "فطَّره" when he split it into pieces, repeating the action in it. Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "Here it is closer to the meaning", that is, the shadda. "يَتَفَطَّرْنَ" is in the position of the accusative as the khabar of "تكادُ". Al-Akhfash claimed it here has the sense of "intending", and recited:
326 - 0- كادَتْ وكِدْتُ وتلك خيرُ إرادةٍ ... لو عادَ مِنْ زمنِ الصَّبابةِ ما مَضَى
(She was about to, and I was about to, and that was the best of intentions, if what has passed of the time of passion could return.)
His saying "هَدَّاً" has three views. One: it is a maṣdar in the position of ḥāl, that is "demolished", on the basis that this maṣdar is from هدَّ زيدٌ الحائطَ يَهُدُّه هَدَّاً, that is, he demolished it. Two, the view of Abū Jaʿfar: it is a maṣdar not of the same root, since it is in its meaning, because "الخُرور" is falling and demolition, and this is on the basis that it is from هَدَّ الحائطُ يَهِدُّ, that is, "the wall collapsed", so it is intransitive. Three: it is a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose). Al-Zamakhsharī said: "that is: because they are demolished."

semin-durr:91-91.t:
His saying: {أَن دَعَوْا}: Its position has five views. One: it is in the position of the accusative as mafʿūl li-ajlihi; so said Abū l-Baqāʾ and al-Ḥawfī, without making clear what the governing word in it is. The governing word may be "تكاد", "تَحِزُّ" or "هَدَّاً", that is "they are demolished because they called"; but the condition for the accusative in them is lacking, namely sameness of agent between the object of purpose and its governing word. If they meant it is on omission of the lām - and omission of the lām is regular with "أنْ" - then it is close. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It may be accusative on the supposition of dropping the lām and the verb reaching it, that is 'هدَّاً لأَنْ دَعَوْا', giving the falling-down as the reason for the demolishing, and the demolishing as caused by their calling a son for the Merciful." This is his explicit statement that it is by omission of the preposition and is not strictly an object of purpose.
Second view: it is genitive after omission of the preposition, as is the school of al-Khalīl and al-Kisāʾī.
Third: it is a badal for the pronoun in "مِنْه", as in:
326 - 1- على حالةٍ لو أنَّ في القومِ حاتماً ... على جودِهِ لضَنَّ بالماءِ حاتِمِ
(In a state in which, were Ḥātim among the people, even Ḥātim with all his generosity would be stingy with water.)
with the last "حاتم" in the genitive as a badal for the hā' in "جودِه". The Shaykh said: "This is far-fetched, because of the great separation between the substitute and what it replaces by two sentences."
Fourth: it is nominative as agent of "هَدَّاً". Al-Zamakhsharī said: "that is: the calling of a son for the Merciful demolished them." The Shaykh said: "There is remoteness in this, because the apparent sense of 'هَدَّاً' is a corroborating maṣdar, and a corroborating maṣdar does not govern; and if we supposed it non-corroborating, it would not govern by analogy unless it was a command or an interrogative, such as 'ضَرْباً زيداً' and 'أضَرْباً زيداً', with a disagreement on it. As for when it is a statement, as al-Zamakhsharī posited, 'that is: the calling of a son for the Merciful demolished them', it is not analogical; what has come of this is rare, like the saying of Imruʾ al-Qays:
326 - 2- وُقوفاً بها صَحْبِيْ عليَّ مطيَّهم ... يقولون: لا تَهْلَِكَ أَسَىً وتجمَّلِ
(My companions halted their mounts over me there, saying: 'Do not perish of grief; show fortitude.')
that is: 'my companions halted'."
Fifth: it is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, whose implied form is: "What necessitates that is their calling"; so Abū l-Baqāʾ posited.
"دَعا" may have the sense of "named", and so take two objects, the second of which may be governed by the bā'. The poet said:
326 - 3- دَعَتْنِي أخاها أمُّ عمروٍ ولم أكنْ ... أخاها ولم أَرْضَعْ بلَبانِ
(Umm ʿAmr called me her brother, though I was not her brother nor suckled at the same breast.)
دَعَتْني أخاها بعد ما كان بينَنا ... من الفعلِ ما لا يَفْعَلُ الأَخَوانِ
(She called me her brother after there had passed between us such deeds as two brothers do not do.) And the saying of another:
326 - 4- ألا رُبَّ من يُدْعَى نَصيحاً وإنْ يَغِبْ ... تَجِدْه بغَيْبٍ منكَ غيرَ نَصِيْحِ
(Many a one is called a sincere adviser, but if he is absent you find him, in your absence, not sincere.)
The first of the two objects in the verse is omitted. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "seeking generality and inclusion of everything for which a son is claimed." It may also be from "دعا" with the sense of "ascribed", whose muṭāwiʿ is in the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Whoever lays claim to other than his masters (من ادَّعَى إلى غير مَوالِيه)", and the saying of the poet:
326 - 5- إنَّا بني نَهْشَلٍ لا نَدَّعِيْ لأَبٍ ... عنه ولا هو بالأَبْناءِ يَشْرِيْنا
(We, the sons of Nahshal, do not claim descent from a father other than him, nor does he buy us with sons.) that is: we do not trace our lineage to him.

semin-durr:92-92.t: {يَنبَغِي} is the imperfect of انْبَغَى. انْبَغَى is the muṭāwiʿ of بَغَى, that is "he sought", and {أَن يَتَّخِذَ} is its agent. Ibn Mālik counted "يَنْبَغي" among the verbs that are not conjugated. This is rejected against him, for the past form has been heard of it: they said "انْبَغَى".

semin-durr:93-93.t:
His saying: {مَن فِي السماوات}: "مَنْ" may be an indefinite noun qualified by an adjective, its adjective being the prepositional phrase after it. Abū l-Baqāʾ mentioned only that, and so did al-Zamakhsharī, but the apparent wording of the latter implies that nothing else is permissible, for he said: "'مَنْ' is qualified; it occurs after every indefinite as it occurs after 'رُبَّ' in his saying:
326 - 6- رُبَّ مَنْ أنضجْتُ غيظاً صدرَه ...
(How many a one whose breast I have cooked with rage...)" End. It may also be a relative. The Shaykh said: "that is: 'not all of that which is in the heavens'; and 'كُلٌّ' enters on 'الذي' because it comes for the genus, as in His saying {والذي جَآءَ بالصدق وَصَدَّقَ بِهِ} [al-Zumar: 33] and like it:
326 - 7- وكلُّ الذي حَمَّلْتني أَتَحَمَّلُ ...
(And all that you have burdened me with, I bear.)" He means that the relative must be interpreted as general so that the annexation of "كل" to it is sound; and whenever a particular, specific individual is meant by it, annexing "كل" to it is impossible.
{آتِي الرحمن} is the khabar of "كلُّ", made singular in accordance with its wording; had it been pluralised it would have been permissible, and it was mentioned at the beginning of this topic that whenever it is annexed to a definite noun both ways are permissible. Al-Suhaylī spoke on that, saying: "'كُلٌّ', when it begins a sentence and is annexed in wording - meaning to a definite noun - it is not good except to make the khabar singular, following the sense. You say 'كلُّكم ذاهبٌ', that is, each one of you is going; so this matter stands in the Qur'an, ḥadīth and eloquent speech. If you say that in His saying {وَكُلُّهُمْ آتِيهِ} [Maryam: 95] it is only a following of the wording because it is a singular noun, we say: rather it is a noun of plurality, and a collective noun is not predicated of with a singular. You say 'القومُ ذاهبون' and not 'ذاهبٌ', even though the word 'القوم' is a singular word. 'كلُّكم ذاهب' is good only because they say 'كلُّ واحدٍ منكم ذاهبٌ', so the singular follows this meaning."
The Shaykh said: "'كلُّكم ذاهبون' and the like need hearing and transmission from the Arabs." This confirms what al-Suhaylī said. I say: calling the singular a following of the meaning is contrary to the technical usage; rather that is following the wording, and the plural is following the meaning.
Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "'آتِي' is made singular in accordance with the wording of 'كل', and it has been made plural in another place in accordance with its meaning." I say: his saying "in another place", if he means in the Qur'an, the plural occurs only with "وكلٌّ" cut off from annexation, such as {كُلٌّ فِي فَلَكٍ يَسْبَحُونَ} [al-Anbiyāʾ: 33] and {وَكُلٌّ أَتَوْهُ دَاخِرِينَ} [al-Naml: 87]; and if he means elsewhere, it needs hearing from the Arabs, as already stated.
The majority annex "آتِي" to "الرحمن". ʿAbdallāh ibn al-Zubayr, Abū Ḥaywa, Ṭalḥa and a group read it with tanwīn and "الرحمن" in the accusative.
"عَبْداً" and "فَرْداً" are accusative as ḥāl.

semin-durr:96-96.t: His saying: {وُدّاً}: The majority read it with ḍamma on the wāw. Abū l-Ḥārith al-Ḥanafī read it with fatḥa, and Janāḥ ibn Ḥubaysh with kasra. It may be that the fatḥa form is a maṣdar, and the ḍamma and kasra forms are nouns.

semin-durr:97-97.t:
His saying: {بِلِسَانِكَ}: it may be attached to an omitted element as ḥāl. "اللِّسان" here is the language, that is, "We sent it down in your tongue". It has also been said that it has the sense of "on" (ʿalā), which is unneeded and indeed has no apparent meaning.
"لُدَّاً" is the plural of "أَلَدّ", which is one intensely contentious, like الحُمْر, the plural of أَحْمر.

semin-durr:98-98.t:
The people read "تُحِسُّ" with ḍamma on the tā' and kasra on the ḥā', from أَحَسَّ. Abū Ḥaywa, Abū Jaʿfar and Ibn Abī ʿAbla read "تَحُسُّ" with fatḥa on the tā' and ḍamma on the ḥā'. Some read "تَحِسُّ" with fatḥa and kasra, from حَسَّه, that is, "he perceived it", from which "the five senses" (الحواسُّ الخَمس).
"منهم" is a ḥāl from "أحد", since it was originally an adjective of it, and "مِنْ أحدٍ" is an object in which "مِنْ" was added.
Ḥanẓala read "تُسْمَعُ" with ḍamma on the tā' and fatḥa on the mīm, as a passive; "رِكْزاً" is an object in both readings, except that it is a second object in the anomalous reading. "الرِّكْزُ" is a faint sound, without articulation of letters or by the mouth, from which "رَكَزَ الرمحَ", that is, he hid its tip in the ground and concealed it, and from it "الرِّكاز", which is buried wealth, because of its concealment and hiddenness. They recited:
326 - 8- فَتَوَجَّسَتْ رِكْزَ الأنيسِ فَرَاعَها ... عن ظهر غَيْبٍ، والأَنِيْسُ سَقامُها
(She sensed the faint sound of a human, and it startled her, from the unseen, and the human is her bane.)
